# SWCraft 0.14.0

**Released 2026-10-08** (the bump commit; the tag follows the `verify` gate on both self-hosted
runners, Linux and Windows, on this commit, and the tag's own run publishes the release archives to
the NAS). This note was written with each change rather than after it, so every figure
below was measured on the host and at the commit that produced it.

## The generated file keeps every value the model holds, and an import names every value it does not carry

Until this release the ARXML SWCraft wrote could differ from the model it was written from, and an
import could leave out part of an export without a word. Descriptions were never written; a timing
event's period and a runnable's minimum start interval were rounded to whole milliseconds, so a
period of 0.5 ms or less was written as `0`; a value type's `value_min` and `value_max` were not
written at all; every member of a record or an array was written with the category `VALUE`, a record
or an array included; an application type's conversion named no unit; every receiver carried a
`FILTER` that the standard allows only on integers; an argument typed by an array stated the opposite
of what an absent setting means for it; and two attributes every com-spec must carry were missing.

The rule now is the one this release is measured against: **the writer changes no value the model
holds and writes every value the model holds for which ARXML has a place, and an import carries each
value of the export or names it in the report.**

**How that is checked.** SWCraft's own test suite imports real tool exports the maintainer holds privately,
generates ARXML from the result, and compares the export with the generated
file element by element, ignoring order. Every difference must be one of four things: a value the
import report names; the same meaning spelled another way, where the standard's text says the two
mean the same — a number written in another notation, an empty wrapper element left out; a choice
the standard leaves open and SWCraft states as its own — its package layout, and an empty
description read as none; or something SWCraft adds that the export did not state, legal in the
standard and SWCraft's choice — a com-spec for a client port, SWCraft's own metadata, the
implementation element every component gets. Those four are a fixed list of 23 kinds of difference,
each with the condition it holds under and the text of the standard it rests on, and anything else
fails the comparison.

**The list was read against the standard before this release.** Every kind of difference now cites
the sentence of the AUTOSAR text that grounds it, read in the 4.2.2 and the 4.3.0 documents.
Six kinds the text does not ground were removed, among them an absent port API option read as one
with both features off. Three kinds were
narrowed to what the text supports:

- **Numbers.** Two numbers are compared as numbers only where the schema types the field as a
  number, and each is read in the notation the schema gives that field.
- **Empty elements.** An empty element may be left out only where the schema makes it a wrapper, or
  where it is one of three objects whose every attribute is optional.
- **Scale limits.** A scale limit may be left out only where it is infinite on its own side. SWCraft
  now carries the finite ones.

Two kinds are now classed as SWCraft's own choice rather than the standard's meaning: the package
layout, and an empty description read as none. The comparison found four things to fix in SWCraft
itself, each below:

- an octal number was read as decimal;
- a scale's limits were not carried;
- a port API option with both features off was dropped without a line;
- a sign followed by a space was not read as a sign.

**What the generated file now carries:**

- **Every description.** A `description` is written as the element's `DESC` on every element
  SWCraft writes — components, ports, runnables, compositions, their members, connectors and
  delegations, both interface kinds, data elements, operations and arguments, every data type, a
  record's fields, an implementation record's elements, mapping sets, and the units, computation
  methods and data constraints of the data description — and an enumeration literal's on its
  computation scale. The text is written exactly as the file holds it, spaces and line breaks
  included, as one paragraph marked as applying to every language (`FOR-ALL`); only an empty
  description writes nothing. An external element writes nothing at all, so its description has no
  place in the file.
- **A composition's title** is written as its long name whenever it differs from the name, and an
  import reads a long name back exactly as the export spelled it, a blank one included. A
  composition with no long name still takes its name as its title.
- **Exact timing.** A period and a minimum start interval are written as the number the model holds,
  in seconds, with no rounding. Every value on the old millisecond grid is written with the same
  digits as before, so no generated file of a model on that grid changes.
- **A value type's bounds**, written as the type's own data constraint `{name}_Range` beside the
  type, and read back by an import. A value type's `unit` has no place in the standard's table for an
  implementation type and is still not written.
- **A member's category is its type's** — `STRUCTURE` for a record, `ARRAY` for an array, `VALUE`
  otherwise — as the standard requires of an array element.
- **A conversion names its unit.** The computation method of an application type's conversion now
  refers to the type's unit, which the standard requires of a linear conversion. A conversion with no
  unit is therefore refused; *Upgrading a project* has the one-line repair.
- **No receiver filter.** No `FILTER` is written: the model states none, and an absent filter means
  no filtering. An export's `FILTER` of type `ALWAYS` — which every receiver of a file written by an
  earlier SWCraft carries — means the same and is imported without a line.
- **The two missing com-spec attributes.** Every sender and receiver com-spec now carries
  `HANDLE-OUT-OF-RANGE NONE` and every non-queued receiver `HANDLE-TIMEOUT-TYPE NONE`, each the value
  that asks for no mechanism, because the standard requires both and gives neither a default. The
  other attributes a com-spec must carry are still written with their no-mechanism value when the
  model is silent.
- **An argument typed by an array** carries no `SERVER-ARGUMENT-IMPL-POLICY`: absent, the standard
  reads it as the array's base type, which is what SWCraft means. Every other argument still states
  `USE-ARGUMENT-TYPE`, which an absent setting would mean too.

**Five values the model did not hold are carried now** — whether an interface is a service
interface, a data element's queuing policy and its calibration access, a port's com-spec attributes
that differ from the defaults, and the modes in which a timing event does not start its runnable.
Each is an optional field (the contract section below lists them with their checks), absent unless
the export states it, and each is written back as stated.

**Every other value an import does not carry is now a line of the report**, under *Not supported by
SWCraft* unless a rule of the standard makes it a defect of the export. A value equal to what
SWCraft's generated file states for the element — the standard's default where SWCraft writes
nothing, or the no-mechanism value it writes — is carried by being equal and gets no line, which is
why a file SWCraft wrote imports with none of them. The lines fall into two kinds, and `swcraft
import component` treats them differently:

- **A value that changes what an RTE or an integrator does** stops `swcraft import component`, as
  every skipped line always has: an operation's possible errors and an application error, a com-spec
  attribute or a whole com-spec SWCraft does not carry, a disabled mode on another kind of event or
  through a port the import skipped, an argument's `SERVER-ARGUMENT-IMPL-POLICY` that means something
  other than what SWCraft writes, a value type's range SWCraft cannot read, a property of a type's
  definition it does not read, a `MEASUREMENT-POINT` policy, and a linear conversion's scale limit it
  cannot read.
- **A value that documents or annotates** is printed and passed: `swcraft import component` lists it
  in the preview and under `--dry-run` in a block of its own, *Not carried from the file*, and goes
  on. That is a value specification's label, an element's other documentation (short name fragments,
  long name, introduction, annotations) and its `UUID`, a package's own content, a calibration access
  on anything but a data element, a description in a second language or holding markup, and a
  generated element's name the import cannot keep.

**External elements take their own names more often.** An external interface or type the import
writes for a reference into another file used to take the `_ext` suffix whenever any element the
export declares held its name, imported or not. It now judges the name against the names its own
layer of the project really carries; the whole rule is under *An interface or a type from another
file of the delivery is imported as an external element*, below. An external
interface still takes `_ext` where an imported interface or another external interface
holds its name. The import of SWCraft's own generated file gives every
external element the same name again.

**What this does not reach:**

- **Only the real tool exports the maintainer holds privately were measured.** The fixed list of differences was drawn from them, and a
  kind of difference none of them shows is not on it: another export can fail the comparison where
  these pass. A kind the list holds by hand-built files alone rests on the standard's text, not on
  an export.
- **A number is compared exactly, and text as written.** The standard allows a tolerance when it
  compares two numbers; the comparison does not, and it claims no same meaning for text.
- **A report line is checked to exist, not to be right.** A difference the import report names is
  allowed when a line stands at its place; what the line says is held by the report's own tests.
- **The comparison is SWCraft's own test, not a check you run.** It proves those exports, not
  your project.
- **SWCraft writes a component's ports in its own order**, not the export's, and a value type's
  `unit` and a component's memory budget have no place in the file; none of the three is compared.
- **A description is one paragraph.** A second language or inline markup in an export is named, not
  carried, and SWCraft writes no introduction of its own.
- **A component file written by SWCraft 0.13.0 or earlier** that reaches an array-typed argument, or
  states an enumeration's initial value as a number, is now refused by `swcraft import component`:
  *If you exchange component files*, below, has the repair.

## The data types live in seven directories of their own

Every earlier release kept a model's data types in one directory, `data_types/`, every kind side by
side, and its mapping sets in a `mapping_sets/` beside it. AUTOSAR does not see them that way: an
application type, an implementation type and a base type are three different things, a mapping set
pairs the first two, and an application type and an implementation type routinely carry **one
name** — one for the physical meaning, one for the bits. In one directory they could not, so an
import renamed the implementation member `{name}_impl` and a hand-written model had to
invent a second name.

Now the data description lives in seven directories under `model/data_types/`, each a layer of its
own:

| Directory | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `data_types/application/` | application types: `enum`, `record`, `array`, `application_type` |
| `data_types/implementation/` | implementation types: `value_type`, `reference_type`, `implementation_record`, `implementation_array`, `pointer`, `external_type` |
| `data_types/base/` | base types (`base_type`) |
| `data_types/mapping_sets/` | mapping sets (no longer `mapping_sets/` at the model root) |
| `data_types/units/` | units — new, below |
| `data_types/compu_methods/` | computation methods — new, below |
| `data_types/constraints/` | data constraints — new, below |

A model has fifteen layers. `swcraft init` creates every directory, and each may stay empty.

**A data element or an argument says which side its type is on.** The single `type:` key is gone: an
element names its type by `implementation_type:` or by `application_type:`, exactly one of the two,
because one name may now be declared in both layers and SWCraft does not guess the side:

```yaml
data_elements:
  - name: VehicleSpeed
    implementation_type: VehicleSpeed_T
```

A file that still says `type:` is refused when it is read, naming the element: *data element
'VehicleSpeed' must declare exactly one of 'application_type' and 'implementation_type'*.

**A type keeps its name on both sides.** An application type and an implementation type of one name
are two elements, one per layer; an import writes both under the name the export declares them with,
and the report's `{name}_impl` lines are gone. A base type and an implementation type of one name are both imported too, and a value type may
rest on a base type of its own name; the import used to refuse that pair. Merge and conflict lines in
the import report name the layer: `application_types/…`, `implementation_types/…`, `base_types/…`.

**Every data type's path in the generated ARXML changed.** `/DataTypes` holds no element of its own
any more: each layer's elements are written into a package of their own — `/DataTypes/Application`,
`/DataTypes/Implementation`, `/DataTypes/Base`, `/DataTypes/Units`, `/DataTypes/CompuMethods`,
`/DataTypes/Constraints` and `/DataTypes/MappingSets` — and every reference names that path. A form
SWCraft generates for a type (`{name}_Unit`, `{name}_Compu`, `{name}_Range`, `{enum}_CompuMethod`)
lies beside its type, in the type's package, and an element's `package` is one sub-package below its
layer's package. A model with no data type writes the bytes it wrote. Every other model's ARXML file
differs from 0.13.0's in those paths, and in nothing else that this change makes: the content of
every element is the same, checked on every committed project.

**Names that became legal.** Because each layer has a package of its own, several names no longer
collide: a mapping set named like a data type or a generated form; a type of one layer under a name
SWCraft generates in another (a value type named `{enum}_CompuMethod`, a base type named
`{app}_Unit`); a base type and a value type of one name; and an application type and an
implementation type of one name, each with inline bounds generating its own `{name}_Range` in its own
package. `swcraft import model` no longer renames a mapping set. Two elements of **one** layer still
may not share a name, and the four checks that report a declared type named like a form SWCraft
generates still refuse it inside the form's own package.

**Retired checks.** Eleven checks can no longer fire and are gone, each shown unreachable before it
was removed: the mapping set named like a data type, and the ten that reported a reference to a type
of the wrong kind — a data element, an argument, a record field or an array element naming a base
type; a value type whose base is not a base type; a record's or an array's member naming an
implementation type; and a reference type's base, an implementation record's element, an
implementation array's element or a pointer's target naming no implementation type. Each role now
names a layer, so a reference into the wrong one simply finds nothing. A model that met one of them now meets that role's check for
an undeclared type: a data element naming a base type, for instance, is reported as naming no type.

**`list`, `query` and `impact` name the new layers.** `swcraft list` takes `application_types`,
`implementation_types`, `base_types`, `mapping_sets`, `units`, `compu_methods` and
`data_constraints`; `swcraft list data_types` is a usage error now (exit 2). `swcraft impact` and
`swcraft query` name a node by its layer's token — `application_type`, `implementation_type`,
`base_type`, `mapping_set`, `unit`, `compu_method`, `data_constraint` — where they said `data_type`,
and walk the seven references a type makes to a unit, a computation method or a data constraint. The
assistant's server reaches all fifteen layers through the same tools as before.

**What this does not reach:**

- **Nothing converts a project on the old layout.** A model with an element file directly in
  `data_types/` or in a `mapping_sets/` at the model root is refused on every read, a git revision
  in that layout included; *Upgrading a project* below gives the four steps and the sentence.
- **A file exported by an earlier release** places its types at `/DataTypes/{name}` or
  `/DataTypes/{package}/{name}`. Both imports read it by the element's kind, so every type lands in
  its layer, but a `package` it states is not recovered and no line says so.
- **A bare pair collapses, as before.** Where an export declares an application type and an
  implementation type of one name with nothing but a plain mapping between them, the import still
  keeps the one implementation type and lists the pair in its report — a few such lines on a real tool
  export. Nothing is lost: the generated file writes the pair again.
- **An external type stub** is judged against the implementation types alone, so an application
  type or a base type of its name no longer gives it an `_ext` suffix, and it may then take a `~1` file name. The
  whole rule is under *An interface or a type from another file of the delivery is imported as an
  external element*, below.
- **Two kinds of one layer** still cannot share a name; inside the application layer the import
  gives one of them an `_app` suffix.
- **A repeated type name.** Where a model declares one name twice in one layer — which the
  duplicate-name check already reports — the checks of a type's role, its initial values and its
  mapping set judge the first declaration in the order SWCraft reads the files.

## A unit, a conversion and a data constraint are elements several types share

An application type stated its `unit`, its `conversion` and its `range` inline, and an enumeration
its `literals`; SWCraft wrote one private `UNIT`, `COMPU-METHOD` or `DATA-CONSTR` per type. An
export can share them: one unit or one table named by many types. An import could not keep that sharing
and turned every shared form into copies, with a line for each. Now three kinds of element exist, one
layer each:

```yaml
# data_types/units/KmPerHour.yaml
name: KmPerHour
display_name: km/h

# data_types/compu_methods/Speed_Linear.yaml
name: Speed_Linear
kind: linear
unit: KmPerHour
factor: 0.1

# data_types/compu_methods/GearPosition.yaml
name: GearPosition
kind: texttable
entries:
  - name: Park
    value: 0
  - name: Drive
    value: 1

# data_types/constraints/Speed_Limits.yaml
name: Speed_Limits
min: 0
max: 300
```

- A **unit** has a `display_name`, a `description` and a `package`, and no `kind` key.
- A **computation method** is a `texttable` — one or more `entries`, each a `name`, an integer
  `value` and an optional `description` — or a `linear`: the `unit` it names (required), a `factor`
  (default 1) and an `offset` (default 0).
- A **data constraint** has an optional `min`, `max` and integer `level`, the lower not above the
  upper, and no `kind` key.

**A conversion states the stored values it applies to.** A `linear` and an application type's inline
`conversion` may carry `limits`: a `lower` and an `upper` bound, each a `value` on the stored side with
an `interval` of `closed` (the default) or `open`. The generated ARXML writes them as the lower and upper
limit of the conversion's scale, which the standard reads as the values the conversion is defined
for — not the type's `range`, which says which physical values are valid. The lower bound may not be
above the upper one, and the two may be equal only when both are `closed`; a file that says otherwise
is refused when it is read. An import carries a `LINEAR` scale's limits as stated; a limit infinite on
its own side is the absent bound, with a descriptive line; a pair is carried whole or not at all, so a
limit that cannot be read leaves both uncarried, with a skipped line for each limit stated. **Two types whose conversions differ only in their
limits are no longer interface-compatible**: a connector or a delegation between ports whose data
elements are typed so is reported, as a different range already was. Finite
limits are carried, and infinite ones are the absent bound. `interval` is written in a model file even at its default, `closed`. A `limits` that
states neither bound (`limits: {}`) is the same as none: no limit is written for it, and it compares
equal to a conversion without them.

A type names one by reference: an application type by `unit_ref`, `compu_method_ref` (a `linear`)
and `data_constr_ref`; an enumeration, a value type and a reference type by `compu_method_ref` (a
`texttable`). The inline form stays beside them, each exclusive with its reference: an application
type states at most one of `unit` and `unit_ref`, of `conversion` and `compu_method_ref`, of `range`
and `data_constr_ref`, and an enumeration exactly one of `literals` and `compu_method_ref`. The
generated ARXML writes each element once, in its layer's package, and every type that names it
references that one element.

**An implementation type's table.** A value type or a reference type may name a `texttable`, and the
generated ARXML writes its `COMPU-METHOD-REF`, so the named values an RTE generates for it survive an
import and a write. Its initial values are the table's entry names (see *An initial value is written
in the form its type asks for*).

**What `swcraft check-model` reports**, and `swcraft generate arxml` refuses with nothing written:
a reference to an element that is not declared; a computation method of the wrong kind for the type
that names it; a reference type's table on a chain that does not end in a value type; an entry name
or value repeated in one table; two units, two computation methods (a `texttable` and a `linear`
included) or two data constraints of one name; a type stating both forms of one property; an empty
table; a blank name or reference; and a data constraint whose `min` is above its `max`, which is
refused while the file is read, as an inline `range` is. An application type's `conversion` needs a
unit, stated as `unit` or as `unit_ref`. Twenty-eight checks arrive with the three layers. A text
XML cannot carry is now looked for in a unit's `display_name` and in every element's and table
entry's `description` as well. `{enum}_CompuMethod` is reserved only for an enumeration that states
`literals`: one that names a table generates no such form, so the name is free; and an element may
carry the name of a form SWCraft generates for a type, because the two lie in different packages.

**Importing.** `swcraft import model` creates an element for every unit, computation method and data
constraint the export states in a shape SWCraft holds, under the export's name, and each type names
it: a form two types share is one element and two references.
A shape SWCraft does not hold is not created and is one
skipped line — a unit stating an SI relation, a computation method stating its physical-to-internal
direction, a table that cannot be an enumeration, a constraint with several rules or internal limits
— and what an element has no place for is a line too (an enumeration's unit or range, a table's
own unit). **A project's own generated form reads back inline**: a form in its type's own package,
named `{type}_Unit`, `_Compu`, `_Range` or `_CompuMethod`, referenced by that type alone and stating
nothing the inline field cannot, is read into the type's inline field; every other form is an
element. The report's lines about shared forms not carried, about a form's name SWCraft would give it
itself, about an implementation type's table and about a constraint's level are gone, because the
model now holds what they named. A `LINEAR` scale
that states a label moved to *Defects of the export*: the standard's table of attributes by category makes a scale's label not applicable to that
category, at 4.2.2 and at 4.3.0 (`[constr_1375]`).

**One name declared twice.** A unit, a computation method or a data constraint the export declares
twice takes the verdict a type takes: equal declarations merge, differing ones conflict and neither is
imported. A type's comparison holds the reference, so two declarations of a type naming two
differently named forms of equal content conflict. A computation
method name declared twice with different scales conflicts, the implementation pair naming it
conflicts with it, and the mapping set entries naming that pair keep an unresolved reference each.
**A `--packages` selection that holds a conflict does not generate until the export is repaired**:
the source is its maker's to fix, and SWCraft picks no side.

**What this does not reach:**

- **The inline form stays private.** Two hand-written types spelling one unit inline still write two
  `UNIT` elements; sharing is what the elements are for.
- **What an element cannot say.** A `linear` holds no scale label and one direction (internal to
  physical) — its scale limits it does hold, below; a unit holds no SI factor, offset or physical dimension, so whether two
  units are compatible is not judged; no computation method category beyond `TEXTTABLE` and `LINEAR`,
  no internal constraint, and no `data_constr_ref` on a value type, whose bounds stay inline with
  their `{name}_Range`. A data constraint's `level` is compared by no check.
- **A form read back inline** is recognised by its place, its name and its single referrer, so a
  foreign file laid out in exactly SWCraft's shape is read the same way and its author's form is held
  inline rather than as an element; written back, it lands at the same path, name and content.
- **The five other categories** the standard's table makes unable to carry a scale label, and a
  computation method with no category, keep their label line under *Not supported by SWCraft*.
  A label changes no behaviour.
- **A reference type whose chain ends in a record** keeps its `compu_method_ref` on import with no
  report line, and `swcraft check-model` then reports it — the export's defect, carried as it
  stands. A chain ending at an external type is not judged.
- **No change set reaches the duplicate checks**: the assistant's server refuses a project that holds
  one name twice in one layer before any check runs.

## An initial value is written in the form its type asks for

A data element's `init`, and a port's own `init` on a `com_specs` entry, used to be written into the
generated ARXML as a number whatever the element's type was — an enumeration's value as the number of
its literal, an application type's value in the form an implementation type takes. Now each value is
written in the form the standard asks for its type:

- under an **application type**, as an application value — one value, the category `VALUE`, with
  the type's own unit, the same unit element the type itself references, where the type states one;
- under an **enumeration**, as its literal's **text**, at every level: the element's own value and a
  member of a record or an array value alike;
- under a **value type or a reference type that references a table** (a `compu_method_ref` naming a
  `texttable` computation method, first one down the type's chain), as a text value naming the
  table's entry. In the model such a value is written exactly as under an enumeration — the entry's
  name:

  ```yaml
  # model/interfaces/IHeadlamp.yaml
  name: IHeadlamp
  kind: sender_receiver
  data_elements:
    - name: Beam
      implementation_type: HeadlampMode_T   # a value type whose compu_method_ref names a table
      init: LowBeam
  ```

  A number there is refused — by `swcraft check-model`, by the assistant's edits and by the
  generator, with nothing written — under the check that already refused an unknown literal of an
  enumeration.

A number inside a record or an array value stays in the numerical form it had, because the standard
prescribes no form for a member. A value under an implementation type with no table, and a model
that states no `init` at all, are written exactly as before. So **the generated ARXML of every model
with an application-typed or an enumeration-typed `init` changes**, and no other model's does.

**Importing.** `swcraft import model` and `swcraft import component` now judge each initial value by
the **file's own** types, and no longer read a number as an enumeration literal:

- the form the standard asks for is carried;
- an element's own value of the wrong form — an enumeration's value given as a number — is not
  carried, and is one line under *Defects of the export* citing `[constr_1221]`;
- an enumeration **member** of a record or an array value given as a number is not carried, and is
  one line under *Not supported by SWCraft*;
- a number inside a record or an array value is carried in either form.

A value cannot be held in part, so when one leaf of it is refused the element's whole `init` goes,
and the element starts with no stated `init`. A value whose unit is not its type's is carried, with
one line under *Not supported by SWCraft* — *"the unit of a value is not carried: a value's unit is
its type's"* — which `swcraft import component` lists under *Not carried from the file* and passes.
Where an element is typed in the file by an application type and the import types it by the
implementation type its twin collapsed to, the value is carried in the numerical form that type asks
for, with one line saying so — unless that implementation type references a table, where the value
is not carried and the line says why: SWCraft does not read a number as a literal.

On an import, the values not carried are each a line —
a defect of the export or a value SWCraft does not support — and a port's own
value not carried and a value's unit are lines too.

An enumeration value written as a number is not carried. The import used to carry it as the literal of that
number, and said nothing.

**What this does not reach:**

- **A component file written by an earlier release** states an enumeration's value as a number and
  an application value in the numerical form, so it is judged like any other file: `swcraft import
  component` refuses one that states such a value. Export the component again with this release.
- **An application value of a type that states no unit** is written without one. The standard gives
  a value's unit a multiplicity of 1 and both AUTOSAR schemas admit its absence; SWCraft does not
  invent a unit the model does not hold, so such a file passes the schema check and is not what the
  standard asks for. A type's unit is written, never judged for compatibility with anything.
- **A scale's symbol** is not held: a text under a table that states one is not carried, nor a text
  that equals only a scale's short label.
- **The compound categories, rule-based values and `STRING`** are neither written nor read.
- **The table is found by the first `compu_method_ref`** down a type's chain; a reference that names
  nothing, or a `linear` method, is no table, and its own check reports it.

## The names SWCraft derives can be stated, and an external interface lists what its ports use

### A behaviour, an event and an access point may be named

The generated ARXML names a component's behaviour `{component}_InternalBehavior`, its events
`TMT_…`, `IT_…` and `OIT_…`, and a runnable's access points `R_…`, `W_…` and `Call_…`. An export
names them as its own tool chose, and 0.13.0 dropped every such name on import, with one report line
each. Now a component may state `behavior_name`, and each `timing`, `init` and `operation` event and
each entry of a runnable's `reads`, `writes` and `calls` may state a `name`:

```yaml
name: BrakeController
behavior_name: BrakeController_Behaviour
runnables:
  - name: Monitor
    events:
      - type: timing
        period: 0.01
        name: Cyclic10ms
    reads:
      - port: R_Speed
        element: Speed
        name: ReadSpeed
```

A stated name is written into the generated file **as it is** — no prefix, no number, no change of
case — and everything that refers to it follows: the behaviour's events and the implementation's
reference to it follow a stated behaviour name. Where nothing is stated the name is derived exactly
as before, the event counter still running over every event, so stating one name moves no other;
**a model that states none of these fields generates the same file as before.** `swcraft
check-model` holds a stated name to the AUTOSAR name rules and their 128 characters, judges it with
every other name of its name space ignoring case (below), and reports two events written with one
name. A stated name is also a repair for a generated name that is too long.

**Importing.** Both imports state a behaviour's, an event's and an access point's name wherever the
source's differs from the one SWCraft would derive, and state nothing where it is equal. A source
name that is not a legal AUTOSAR name, or that would be equal ignoring case to another name of its
name space, is not stated: the element keeps the derived name, and its line under *Not supported by
SWCraft* says why. Every other differing name is now stated —
behaviours, events and access points — and the report lines that used to name them
are gone.

**What this does not reach:**

- The model has no place for the other kinds of event, for asynchronous call points, parameter and
  local-variable accesses or mode points, so those cannot be named. A runnable's own name and
  `symbol` are unchanged by this. The diagrams never print these names.
- **A stated name equal to the derived one** says the same thing as stating none, and SWCraft's own
  export of it reads back as stating none. `swcraft import component` compares a stated name as it
  stands, so the unchanged round trip of such a component is reported as a difference. An import
  never states such a name itself.
- An external component states no `behavior_name`: it has no behaviour in the generated file, so
  `swcraft check-model` reports one and the generator refuses it.

### An external interface lists the members its ports use

An external interface stood for an interface another file declares and said nothing about what it
holds, so nothing could be read, written or called through a port on it, and an import skipped every
such access. Now an `external_interface` may list its members by name — `operations` on one whose
`external_dest` is `CLIENT-SERVER-INTERFACE`, `data_elements` on a `SENDER-RECEIVER-INTERFACE` one:

```yaml
# model/interfaces/IBrakeRequest.yaml
name: IBrakeRequest
kind: external_interface
external_ref: /Delivery/Services/Interfaces/IBrakeRequest
external_dest: CLIENT-SERVER-INTERFACE
operations:
  - RequestBrake
```

Through a port on it an `operation` event, a call, a read, a write, a `com_specs` entry and a
`measures` key may then name a listed member, exactly as through a declared interface, and `swcraft
check-model` reports one the list does not hold, naming the external interface and its list. A
name listed twice ignoring case, and a list the `external_dest` does not admit, are refused when the
file is read; a mode-switch or any other external interface lists nothing. The generated file
references a listed member by the external interface's path, a `/`, and the member's name, verbatim,
and writes the port's com-specs from the list as it does for a declared interface: a server com-spec
with a queue length of 1 or a client com-spec per listed operation, a sender or a receiver com-spec
per listed data element, and a `com_specs` entry's attributes on top of it.

**Importing.** Both imports fill the lists with every member the export's ports, events, accesses and
com-specs name exactly one path segment below the external interface, and keep every one of those
that names one. The imports so list operations and data
elements on external interfaces, and keep server, sender and receiver com-specs, call points,
reads, writes and operation events through them.

With the stated names above, the two changes shorten the skipped list of the import report — with, at this release, the descriptive lines
for a scale limit infinite on its own side added (*Upgrading a project*, below).

**What this does not reach:**

- **A listed member is a name, never a definition.** Its type, its arguments and its policy are
  unknown, so the checks of an operation's signature, of queuing, of initial values and of safety
  levels say nothing about it; a `measures` key naming it is accepted and read by no level check.
  A connector across an external interface is still checked for the interface's kind and nothing
  more.
- **A port on an external interface carries com-specs only for what its interface lists.** Such a
  com-spec is never queued; a `com_specs` entry on it may not state `init`, nor, on a require port,
  `queue_length`, and `swcraft check-model` reports either. What is left as report lines: the initial value of com-specs on such ports (there is no type to carry the value
  against; one line each under *Outside the file*, which stops `swcraft import component`), and the
  com-specs of mode-switch external interfaces, which SWCraft does not model in any form —
  each stays a named loss.
- **A member path the list cannot hold** — deeper than one segment, of a kind the `external_dest`
  does not admit, blank, not a legal name, or one of two names alike but for case — is listed by no
  external interface, and whatever names it keeps its line in the report.
- **The lists are written sorted**, so an unsorted list re-imports sorted: the same members, the
  com-specs in another order. A member that only an element dropped later by the import names — a
  `--packages` selection, a skipped component — stays listed.
- **An external interface still never travels in a component file**, with its list or without.
- **The name of an external interface stub** is the last segment of its path; when it takes an
  `_ext` suffix instead is under *An interface or a type
  from another file of the delivery is imported as an external element*, below.

## A runnable names its C symbol, a port carries its own initial value, and no port API option is written

Three things an RTE generator reads from a component were fixed by SWCraft rather than said by the
model: every runnable's entry point was written under the runnable's own name, a port could not
give a data element an initial value other than the element's, and every port was written with a
port API option whose two flags were `false`. The first two are now the model's to say, and the
third is no longer written.

**A runnable's `symbol`.** A runnable may state `symbol`, the C name of its entry point — AUTOSAR's
`SYMBOL`. It is optional; left out, the runnable's name is written, as before:

```yaml
runnables:
  - name: MonitorSpeed
    symbol: Swc_MonitorSpeed_10ms
```

A stated symbol must be a C identifier — a letter or an underscore first, then letters, digits and
underscores, with no length bound — and no two runnables of one component may be written with the
same symbol. `swcraft check-model` reports both, and `swcraft generate arxml`, `--component` and
`--all-components` refuse such a model before they write anything. `swcraft import model` and
`swcraft import component` carry a source `SYMBOL` that differs from the runnable's name, and state
nothing where it is the name.

**A port's own initial value.** A component port's `com_specs` entry may state `init`, the value
this port's com-spec carries for the data element:

```yaml
ports:
  - name: P_Speed
    direction: provide
    interface: IVehicleSpeed
    com_specs:
      - data_element: Speed
        init: 0
```

On that port it takes precedence over the data element's own `init` (`[TPS_SWCT_01182]`,
`[TPS_SWCT_01518]`); an entry without one repeats the element's, as before. The generated ARXML
writes the port's value in place, in the com-spec's own initial value, rather than as a named
constant, and keeps the data element's value and its constant where they were — both in the form
their type asks for (*An initial value is written in the form its type asks for*, above).
`swcraft check-model` judges a port's value by the same checks as a data element's, against the
element's type, and reports an `init` on a queued data element. `swcraft import model` carries a
source com-spec value that differs from its data element's and keeps the element's own value
beside it — 0.13.0 refused both.

**No port API option is written.** The generated ARXML holds no `PORT-API-OPTIONS` any more.
SWCraft's model states no port API option, and an absent option means what an option with both
flags `false` means: the RTE acts on a flag that is `true` only (`[SWS_Rte_02613]`,
`[SWS_Rte_03799]`, `[SWS_Rte_07100]`). So no generated RTE changes — but **every model with a port on
a component produces a different ARXML file**, one option fewer per port; a model without one
produces the same bytes. An import reads an option that states content — argument values, a flag
set to `true`, anything a false/false option does not hold — as a loss, one line per option under
*Not supported by SWCraft*, ending *SWCraft carries no port API option*. An option with both features off requests nothing, but no text
of the standard makes it the same as no option, so it is a line too — a descriptive one, *PORT-API-OPTION
states both of its features off: it requests nothing, and SWCraft carries no port API option*.

**`swcraft import component`** accepts a component whose runnables state their own symbols, and
carries them; a component file an earlier SWCraft wrote — every symbol equal to its runnable's
name, one false/false option per port — imports with one descriptive report line per option.

**No new refusal reaches an existing project.** Every new check reads `symbol` or a port's `init`,
which no earlier model states, so a project that checked clean under 0.13.0 still does, on these
counts. An import never writes a symbol either check refuses: it drops it first and names it (below).

**What this does not reach:**

- **Symbols are unique within one component only.** Two components whose runnables share a symbol
  pass: SWCraft does not carry a component's symbol prefix and knows no ECU, while the standard's
  rule (`[constr_2025]`) is about the components of one ECU instance. A C compiler's limit on an
  identifier's length is not judged. The names of the events SWCraft derives still follow the
  runnable's name, never its symbol.
- **A source symbol is judged as written.** Surrounding spaces, an inner space or a line break make
  it no C identifier; it is then dropped and named, never trimmed. Two runnables of one source
  component stating one symbol lose both symbols and are listed under *Defects of the export*,
  citing `[constr_2025]`; a clash only SWCraft's fallback to a runnable's name would create is
  listed under *Not supported by SWCraft*.
- **A port's own value is a component port's.** On a composition's port, and on a port typed by an
  external interface, it is one report line and not carried. The source's constant name is not
  kept, nor the labels of the source value (one line per com-spec says how many). A port value
  equal to its data element's is not recorded, so a source that repeats the element's value through
  another constant reads as stating none. A sender com-spec on a data element with no initial
  value, whose entry states none, still gets no initial value, although the standard's
  multiplicity is 1. No port value of its own is carried from an import: each one stated is
  one line under *Not supported by SWCraft*.
- **Two round trips report a difference although nothing changed.** A model whose port `init`
  equals its data element's own `init` writes it in place, because the model states it, while an
  import reads a port value equal to the element's as stating none. And a runnable that states a
  `symbol` equal to its own name is written as the same bytes as one that states none, and reads
  back as stating none. `swcraft import component` compares both fields as they stand, so importing
  SWCraft's own export of such a component into the project it came from reports a difference on
  that field. The same holds for a behaviour, event or access point name stated equal to the one
  SWCraft would derive (*The names SWCraft derives can be stated, and an external interface lists what its ports use*, above). Leave such a value out, or take the file's side
  with `--update`.
- **What `swcraft import component` still refuses** of these: a symbol that is no C identifier, two
  runnables written with one symbol, a port API option carrying content, and a port's own value it
  cannot carry — each is a line of the file it cannot import without a loss.
- The port API option's equivalence rests on the RTE specification of R22-11, the one RTE text read;
  that the 4.2.2 and 4.3.0 texts say the same was not checked. `enableTakeAddress`, `indirectAPI`,
  port-defined argument values, error handling and supported features cannot be modelled and stay
  named losses.

## An interface or a type from another file of the delivery is imported as an external element

A real AUTOSAR delivery is split across files, and an export references interfaces and types that
another file of the same delivery declares. 0.13.0 kept the element that made such a reference and
wrote the reference into it as a full AUTOSAR path — and then `swcraft check-model` reported every
one of those paths and `swcraft generate arxml` refused the project, because nothing in the model
could say that the target lies **outside** it. On an export whose only gaps are references of that
kind, the project could not be generated at all without the missing files.

Now such a target is imported as an **external** element: an `external_interface` in `interfaces/`
or an `external_type` in `data_types/implementation/`, a file holding the target's full path and the
kind the reference named, both exactly as the export wrote them. The port, the data element, the
operation argument, the reference type — or an element of an implementation structure or array, or a
pointer's target (below) — that referenced it names the external element, like any other:

```yaml
# model/interfaces/IBrakeRequest.yaml
name: IBrakeRequest
kind: external_interface
external_ref: /Delivery/Services/Interfaces/IBrakeRequest
external_dest: CLIENT-SERVER-INTERFACE
```

The project checks, and it generates. The generated file carries every such reference back exactly
as the source had it — the same path, the same `DEST` — and generates nothing for the external
element itself, so the document is meant to be read together with the files that declare the
targets, as the export was. A port whose interface lives elsewhere is now generated, with the
connectors and delegations on it, and drawn with the shape of its interface's kind. An external
interface may list the operations or data elements its ports use, described above.

The import report says what it did, in three new places, each printed only when it counts something:

```text
STUBBED 3 interface(s), 1 type(s)

External interface stubs (3; declared by no element of this export -- each stub carries the path and DEST verbatim, the reference is written back as the export spelled it, and nothing behind it is imported):
  - /Delivery/Body/Interfaces/ILevel (DEST SENDER-RECEIVER-INTERFACE) -- imported as external stub 'ILevel'
  - /Delivery/Chassis/Interfaces/ILevel (DEST SENDER-RECEIVER-INTERFACE) -- imported as external stub 'ILevel_ext'
  - /Delivery/Services/Interfaces/IBrakeRequest (DEST CLIENT-SERVER-INTERFACE) -- imported as external stub 'IBrakeRequest'

External type stubs (1; declared by no element of this export -- each stub carries the path and DEST verbatim, the reference is written back as the export spelled it, and nothing behind it is imported):
  - /Delivery/Platform/Types/Counter16 (DEST IMPLEMENTATION-DATA-TYPE) -- imported as external stub 'Counter16'
```

An external element takes the last segment of its path as its name. Where that name is already taken
in its own layer — for an external interface, by an interface the import writes, by a name two
conflicting declarations of an interface hold, or by another external interface whose path ends the
same way, as the two `ILevel`s above, which are taken in the order of their paths; for an external
type, by an implementation type the import writes, by a name two conflicting declarations of an
implementation type hold, or by another external type whose path ends the same way — or is a name
Windows reserves for a device, such as `CON` or `AUX`, it takes an `_ext` suffix, and the rename is
listed with the other renames. An application type or a base type of the same name no longer pushes
an external type to `_ext`: the two live in different layers. The third new section,
*DEST disagreements*, lists a path the export references as two different kinds of element; such a
path is not imported as an external element, since one element cannot be both, and it stays under
*Unresolved references*. So does a path that starts with `/DataTypes`, `/PortInterfaces` or
`/ComponentTypes`, the packages the generated ARXML declares the project's own elements in: written
back, the reference would find one of them instead of the other file's. A composition member whose
component type lies at such a path is skipped with a line saying so.

**What an external element does not bring**, deliberately:

- **Its content.** The export does not say what the target declares, and SWCraft does not guess. A
  runnable's reads, writes and calls through a port on an external interface are imported, and may
  be written by hand, only through a member the external interface lists; one through a member it
  does not list is a skipped-element line, and `swcraft check-model` reports it and `swcraft
  generate arxml` refuses it when written by hand. An initial value on a data element whose type is
  external, directly or through reference types, is still not carried.
- **A full compatibility check.** A connector or a delegation across an external interface is checked
  for the interface **kind** its `DEST` names — a client-server one never satisfies a
  sender-receiver port — and for nothing beyond it; where the `DEST` is one of the two general values
  `PORT-INTERFACE` or `DATA-INTERFACE`, not even the kind is known. So the compatibility question the
  assistant can ask never judges a pair across an external interface, whether its kind agrees or is
  unknown: it answers `ok: true` with a reason beginning *not judged: external interface*. Two ports
  that name the same external interface are the exception, because one interface on both ends is
  compatible whatever it declares: that pair answers `ok: true` with an empty reason, as any pair
  sharing one interface does.
- **A level.** An external interface declares no `asil`, and a data element it lists has no level
  either: the checks that compare a producer or a consumer with the level of the signal it handles
  have nothing to compare a port on one against. The assistant asks before it re-points a rated
  consumer's port from a rated interface to an external one, and before it moves a connector or a
  composition's delegation that ends on such a port onto another port of the same component on an
  external interface — a port replaced in the same change by a new one of another name included.
  That question names the moved connections that fit its length and counts the rest, and says the
  consumer interface can no longer be checked, not that the signal is the same; with names so long
  that not even one connection fits, the question is cut short and says how much it left out. A
  declined question's reason repeats the same note without cutting it. It does not ask for a
  providing port, for a port that already names an external interface, for a port replaced by one of
  another name with no connection moved along with it, for a connection whose providing end or
  consuming component changes in the same change, for a connection renamed in the same change it is
  moved or one whose composition changes, for a connection through a composition nested inside
  another, or for a move split across two changes.
- **Every role.** A record field and an array element — of a record or an array, the physical view —
  a value type's base and a mapping set never name an external type, and no application type is ever
  external, because AUTOSAR requires a mapping for one that nothing could supply across a file
  boundary. A reference in one of those roles to something the export does not declare is still
  written as the path and reported by `swcraft check-model`, exactly as in 0.13.0. So is a reference
  to something outside the packages you selected, and a reference to a name the export declares
  twice with different definitions — that one is the source model's to fix.
- **Component files.** `swcraft generate arxml --component` refuses a component whose files reach an
  external element, naming each one with its path, and `--all-components` lists such a component as
  failed: `swcraft import component` could not read that file back. Nor does `swcraft import
  component` replace an external element with the definition a component file brings: a file
  declaring an interface or a type of that name is reported as a conflict.
- **A check on the other file.** Nothing verifies that the delivery really holds the target, that the
  target is what its `DEST` says, or that it declares the members an external interface lists. That
  is for whoever puts the delivery together.

An external element can be written by hand as well, and the editor, the checks and the assistant
treat it like any other element. `swcraft check-model` reports one whose `external_ref` is blank or
not an AUTOSAR path, or starts with `/DataTypes`, `/PortInterfaces` or `/ComponentTypes` (the packages
the generated ARXML declares the project's own elements in, where the reference would find one of
them), or whose `external_dest` is not one AUTOSAR allows there — for an interface one of the eight
port interface kinds, for a type `IMPLEMENTATION-DATA-TYPE` — and the generator refuses it too, with
nothing written.

**The diagrams** draw a port on an external interface with the shape its `DEST` names: the
client-server shapes for `CLIENT-SERVER-INTERFACE`, the sender-receiver shapes for every other kind,
mode-switch included. Resting the pointer on such a port shows `(external)` where a declared port
shows its interface's kind.

## A component declared in another file keeps its connections

A composition in a tool export places components whose type another file of the delivery declares —
the basic software, for one. SWCraft has always imported such a member as an **external
component** (`external: true`, the type's path and kind kept as the export wrote them), but it gave
that component no ports, so every connector and delegation with an end on one was skipped, and every line to the basic
software was missing from the diagrams.

Now an external component declares the ports its connectors reach, each with the **name** and the
**direction** the connector's end states, and those connectors are imported, generated and drawn:

```yaml
# model/swc/external/Dcm.yaml
name: Dcm
external: true
external_ref: /Delivery/Services/Dcm
external_dest: APPLICATION-SW-COMPONENT-TYPE
ports:
  - name: DataServices_Speed
    direction: require
    observed_interface: DataServices_Speed
  - name: GetCurrentTime
    direction: provide
```

Such a port names **no interface**, because the export does not say which one the other file
declares. Where every connector on it came from ports typed by one interface, the import records
that name as `observed_interface` — an observation, used by the diagrams and by `swcraft query`, and
read by no check. The generated file refers to each such port exactly as the export did: the
component's path, the port's name, and the kind of port its direction names.

Of the connectors and delegations with an end
on an external component, those still skipped are skipped — as a defect of the export (the end names a port under a path
that is not the component's own), for a port the export states with two directions, or for a
reason older than this release (a boundary port that was not imported, a duplicate, a repeated
member type, ...). None is skipped any more because the component *"declares no port"*.

After such an import `swcraft check-model` reports nothing, or exactly the findings of the
conflicting declarations the source holds, as before this change; once those are resolved in the
source the whole build — the ARXML validated against the AUTOSAR schema, the documentation and the
diagrams — succeeds on it unedited. The defects are the export's own inconsistency: AUTOSAR requires a connector's end to name a port
of the component it goes through, and these name a port under another path — the same short name in
another package, or another component. SWCraft neither guesses which component was meant nor writes
a reference the export did not make, so each is in the skipped list with that reason, and the report
counts them in a line of their own:

```text
External component stub ports (1 stub(s); name and direction as the connector ends state them, no interface is declared -- an observed interface is the direct neighbours' hint and is never judged):
  - Dcm (/Delivery/Services/Dcm): 2 port(s) -- 0 provide, 2 require; 1 with an observed interface

Stub ports with no observed interface (1; the direct neighbours name different interfaces):
  - Dcm.rAux -- candidates: IOther, ISig

1 connector(s)/delegation(s) reaching an external stub were skipped because the target port path is not owned by the context component's type (R4.2.2 [TPS_GST_00162]) -- a defect of the export; see "Defects of the export" below.
```

The citation names the release the imported file declares — here an export of AUTOSAR 4.2.2 — and
the connectors it counts are listed under *Defects of the export* in the skipped list, described
below.

A fourth block, *Stub ports not imported*, lists a port the export states with two directions: no
port is written for it and every connector reaching it is skipped, because SWCraft does not pick
one. A connector whose end names the port with a segment that is not a valid AUTOSAR name is skipped
the same way, with that reason in the skipped list; and a port name written by hand on an external
component is checked like any other port name, because every connection to the port carries it.

**The diagrams** draw an external component's port with the shape of its observed interface's kind,
and resting the pointer on it shows `(observed)`. Without an observed interface — or when the name
it holds is no longer an interface of the model — the port is drawn with the sender-receiver shapes
and its text ends in `(interface not declared)`.

**What an external component's ports do not give you**, deliberately:

- **A compatibility check.** Nothing in the model says what the other file's port declares, so a
  connection to one is checked for its direction and for nothing else — also when both ends are on
  external components. The compatibility question the assistant can ask answers `ok: true` with a
  reason beginning *not judged: external component*, which is not a statement that the two fit. The
  observed interface never takes part: copying it into `interface` is reported by `swcraft
  check-model`, which accepts no `interface` and no `measures` on an external component's port.
- **More than one hop.** The observed interface comes from the connector's other end only, and is
  kept only when all such ends agree.
- **A level.** The producer-and-consumer safety checks read a port's declared interface, and such a
  port has none, so a signal crossing one is not compared with anything, and a connector moved from a
  rated consumer onto another, external component's port is not asked about. Turning a rated
  component that consumes a rated signal into an external component, which clears its port's
  interface, is asked about first — also when the port is replaced by one of another name and a
  connection into it is moved onto the new one.
- **A check on the other file.** That its component really has the port, in that direction, is the
  export's claim, carried as it stands.

## An enumeration is written with the category `VALUE`

Every earlier release wrote an enumeration as an `APPLICATION-PRIMITIVE-DATA-TYPE` with the category
`TEXTTABLE`. That is a computation method's category, and the standard's table of the categories an
application data type may take (`[constr_1007]`, at 4.2.2 and at 4.3.0) does not list it; neither
AUTOSAR schema checks a category's value, so `swcraft validate` passed it. The 0.13.0 note stated
the defect and left it. Now the enumeration's type is written with the category `VALUE`, and its
`{name}_CompuMethod` keeps `TEXTTABLE`, which is where that category belongs:

```xml
<APPLICATION-PRIMITIVE-DATA-TYPE>
  <SHORT-NAME>Gear_T</SHORT-NAME>
  <CATEGORY>VALUE</CATEGORY>
  ...
<COMPU-METHOD>
  <SHORT-NAME>Gear_T_CompuMethod</SHORT-NAME>
  <CATEGORY>TEXTTABLE</CATEGORY>
```

The category itself changed exactly one line per enumeration in the generated file,
measured on the committed projects that declare an enumeration when it was made; the other changes
of this release to the same file — where the type is declared, an initial value written as the
literal's text — are described in their own sections. The model does not change for it — no field,
no check, no name; the enumeration's description in the editor and in the reference pages now says
`VALUE`.

**Importing.** An export that spells its enumerations `VALUE` — every file
this release writes among them — no longer gets one note per enumeration saying the category would change on
the way out. A file written by SWCraft 0.13.0 or earlier spells them `TEXTTABLE`, so importing
one now prints **one note per enumeration**, *"… CATEGORY 'TEXTTABLE' is imported as an enum -- the
type would be re-exported as CATEGORY 'VALUE'"*. That note is not a regression: the enumeration is
imported whole, with its literals and values, the import succeeds, and the note says only that the
file you generate from it will carry the corrected category. `swcraft import component --update`
over a project that already holds the enumeration reuses it and prints no note.

**What this does not reach:**

- **A tool of your own that reads the generated ARXML** and recognised an enumeration by its type's
  category `TEXTTABLE` stops recognising it. Nothing in SWCraft did — an enumeration is recognised
  by its computation method — but a script or a downstream tool outside SWCraft may have; if yours
  did, make it read the computation method's category instead, which still says `TEXTTABLE`.
- **One file holding both spellings of one enumeration** — an old `TEXTTABLE` declaration and a new
  `VALUE` declaration of the same name, which takes two SWCraft generations joined into one
  document — is listed by `swcraft import model` under *Conflicting declarations*, and neither is
  imported. Remove one of the two from the file, or regenerate the older part with this release,
  before importing.

## A server runnable names the operation that starts it

A runnable could be started by a periodic `timing` event and by the start-up `init` event. A
**server** runnable — the one that answers a client's call — had no event that starts it, so in the
model it stood unattached: the importer skipped every `OPERATION-INVOKED-EVENT` of an export, and a
generator reading SWCraft's ARXML found provided operations that no runnable serves. The export also
wrote every runnable's `CAN-BE-INVOKED-CONCURRENTLY` as `false`, whatever the source said.

Now a runnable's events have a third kind, `operation`, naming one of the component's own `provide`
ports and an operation of that port's client-server interface, and a runnable has `concurrent`:

```yaml
runnables:
  - name: ServeDiagnosticRecords
    concurrent: true             # left out of the file while it is false
    events:
      - type: operation
        port: S_DiagnosticRecords
        operation: GetDiagnosticRecord
```

One runnable may serve several operations, one event each. The generated ARXML writes each as an
`OPERATION-INVOKED-EVENT` named `OIT_{port}_{operation}` — or the `name` the event states (above) —
referencing the runnable, the component's own port and the interface's operation, and writes
`CAN-BE-INVOKED-CONCURRENTLY` from `concurrent`. The derived name is built from the port and the
operation rather than numbered per runnable, so adding one event to a runnable that serves a hundred
renames none of the others.

**What `swcraft check-model` reports**, and `swcraft generate arxml` refuses with nothing written:

- an operation event whose port the component does not declare, whose port is a `require` port or
  names a sender-receiver interface, or whose operation the interface does not declare — on a port
  on an external interface, an operation it does not list;
- one port and operation served twice, by two runnables or twice by one;
- a runnable whose operations could not share one entry point: a different number of arguments, an
  argument of another direction in the same position, or argument types whose structure differs once
  every reference is resolved — an application type or an enumeration compared through the one
  implementation type the component's mapping sets pair it with;
- an event name over the 128-character limit: a port and an operation share **123** characters in the
  derived name, and where two events of one component derive the same name, the numbered name
  counts. A stated `name` is judged on its own.

**What it does not judge**, deliberately, so a clean run is not read as more than it is:

- **Mixed event kinds**: the RTE specification describes mixing as unsupported in explanatory text,
  with no tagged requirement; SWCraft does not judge it. A runnable carrying an operation event beside
  a timing or an init event is read, checked, imported and generated exactly as written, with no
  finding. That the generated file passes the AUTOSAR schema says nothing about whether an RTE
  generator accepts it.
- **The whole of the compatibility constraint.** The check above compares the count, the directions
  and the resolved structure of the arguments. It does not compare the operations' possible errors or
  their return value, how each argument is passed, or argument values a port defines, and an argument
  it cannot resolve completely — an application type the mapping sets pair with no implementation
  type or with two, a type from another file, any operation an external interface lists — is left
  uncompared rather than called compatible.
- **A provided operation no runnable serves.** Not reported, although an RTE generator rejects one.
- **The queue length.** The generated file writes every provided operation's queue length as 1, as
  before.

**Importing.** `swcraft import model` now keeps each server runnable's operation events and its
`concurrent`. An event on a port whose interface the export declares nowhere is kept through the
external interface written for that port, which lists the operation (above); an event the import
cannot bind to a port of the same component and an operation one segment below that port's
interface is a skipped-element line with its reason. A provided operation whose queue length is not
1 is listed under a new heading, *Server queue lengths not carried*; nothing is skipped for it.
A component the import does not write at
all takes its events and its runnables with it. The import writes
application components only: an export's complex-device-driver and service components can
carry more operation events and runnables with `CAN-BE-INVOKED-CONCURRENTLY` `true`.

**Component files.** Every component file this release writes states that it carries operation
events and concurrency, and `swcraft import component --update` reads that statement:

- a file that carries it **replaces** each runnable's operation events and `concurrent`, like the
  rest of the runnable — an operation event the file does not declare is removed;
- a file without it — one 0.13.0 or earlier wrote, which could carry neither, or one another tool
  wrote — **keeps** the project's own operation events and `concurrent` for every runnable the file
  says nothing about, and the report lists what it kept under *OPERATION EVENTS preserved from the
  target project*. Such a file whose only difference is that it says nothing about the project's
  operation events imports as unchanged. A runnable in it that does declare an operation event or
  `concurrent: true` speaks for itself: it is compared and, with `--update`, replaced;
- a file carrying the statement with a value this release does not write is refused, nothing
  written: export the component again.

Timing and init events are compared and replaced as before in every case.

## A structure, an array and a pointer keep their implementation side

The model held the implementation side of a type only for single values — a value type and a
reference type. An implementation **structure**, **array** or **pointer** in an export
(`IMPLEMENTATION-DATA-TYPE` of category `STRUCTURE`, `ARRAY` or `DATA_REFERENCE`) had no kind to land
in, so the import skipped every one of them as an *unsupported category*, and every mapping set entry
that paired a record or an array with one was dropped with it. Now there are three kinds for them,
stored with the other implementation types:

```yaml
# data_types/implementation/MotorCommand_T.yaml
name: MotorCommand_T
kind: implementation_record
elements:
  - name: Left
    type: MotorLevel_T
  - name: Right
    type: MotorLevel_T

# data_types/implementation/Samples_T.yaml
name: Samples_T
kind: implementation_array
element_type: uint16
length: 8
element_name: Element

# data_types/implementation/PduInfoPtr_T.yaml
name: PduInfoPtr_T
kind: pointer
target: PduInfo_T
```

Each names implementation types only — a value type, a reference type, another of the three or an
external type. A reference type may rest on any of them, a data element or an operation argument may
be typed by any of them through `implementation_type`, and a pointer to a pointer is written through
a pointer type of its own. The generated ARXML writes each as one `IMPLEMENTATION-DATA-TYPE` —
`STRUCTURE` with its elements in order, `ARRAY` with a fixed size, `DATA_REFERENCE` with its target —
and a test project holding all three, with their mapping set entries, validates against both AUTOSAR
schemas, 4.2.2 and 4.3.0.

**Mapping sets.** A set may now pair a record with an implementation record and an array with an
implementation array. Such a pair is still **optional**: a record or an array that no set pairs is not
reported. A pair you write is checked in part — matching kinds, as many elements on both sides, each
member matching the element in the same position in kind and shape all the way down, the same array
length — and a pointer is never paired with anything. What the check does **not** judge:

- **member names** — a pair whose two sides name their members differently is accepted, and the
  import keeps both sides' names exactly;
- whether a number's range or conversion fits the type that stores it;
- two members of the same shape in swapped positions;
- a member whose type is external or does not resolve.

**Connections.** Two implementation records are compared element by element with their names, as two
records always were, two implementation arrays by length, element type and the name of their one
element, and two pointers by what they point to. `swcraft check-model` reports a connector
between two application components that carries a data element or an argument typed by a pointer;
one end must be a service or an ECU-abstraction component for a pointer to cross. It does not judge a
pointer inside a structure, an end on an external component, or an end no delegation leads to a
component.

**What `swcraft check-model` reports**, and `swcraft generate arxml` refuses with nothing written: an
element, an array element or a pointer target that names no declared implementation type; an element
name used twice; a pointer that leads back to itself through other types; a mapping set pair the check
above refuses; a pair that names a pointer; and the pointer connector above.

**What these kinds cannot say**, so an import reports it instead: an element declared inline rather
than by a named type, an array whose size varies, a union, a pointer to a function or to `void`, and
a pointer to a pointer declared inline.

**Importing.** `swcraft import model` keeps every implementation structure, array and pointer of the
supported shape, and the mapping set entries that pair them; every other shape is one skipped-element
line saying what it is. Where a record or an array and an implementation structure or array share a
name, both are kept under that name, one in each layer. Records whose fields are arrays, or records
the export declares later, used to be skipped, because the type a field named had not been read yet;
they are imported now, and the interfaces typed by them with them. A pair the check refuses is kept
as the export declares it and listed under a new heading, *Data type maps kept that SWCraft's
composite check refuses*. Checked against real tool exports the maintainer holds privately.

A structure that is the same declaration in two packages is imported once,
and the entry that pairs the second declaration of a record an export declares twice alike is
dropped as already mapped in the set.

## What an import cannot carry from a component's behaviour is named

A component's behaviour in an export holds much more than SWCraft reads: exclusive areas and the
runnables' references into them, per-instance memories and parameters, inter-runnable variables,
service dependencies, implicit data accesses, local-variable and parameter accesses, mode access and
mode switch points, asynchronous call result points, the data type sets a behaviour includes. The
importer used to drop all of it without a line in the report. It now names every item: one
skipped-element line per kind of content, saying which container of a behaviour or of a runnable it
came from and that SWCraft does not read it, and `swcraft import model --verbose` lists each item's
path under its line.

Two things SWCraft does not carry are compared with the source, and a line says where the source
says something SWCraft cannot hold:

- a behaviour's `SUPPORTS-MULTIPLE-INSTANTIATION` that is missing or `true` — the generated ARXML
  writes `false`, and the standard gives the attribute no default;
- a port API option that states content — argument values, a flag set to `true`, a second option
  for one port, or anything else a false/false option does not hold — one line per option,
  ending *SWCraft carries no port API option* (SWCraft writes none, above). An option for a port the
  import does not keep is a line of its own, behind that port's line. An option with both features
  off is a line too, a descriptive one: it requests nothing, so it does not stop `swcraft import
  component`.

A runnable's `SYMBOL` is no longer among them: it is carried (above), and a line names it only when
it cannot be — a symbol that is no C identifier, or one two runnables share. A runnable's symbol and
a port API option's port are read exactly as written, surrounding spaces included; other names and
references are still compared without them. A component whose behaviour is declared more than once
has every behaviour after the first named in one line each; SWCraft reads the first.

Among these lines are the port API options carrying argument values, the implicit data reads and writes, the
per-instance parameters and the parameter accesses. (When this report was first added it named
more, among them the runnable symbols that differ from the runnable's name; those are carried now and their lines
are gone.)

**What the report still does not name**, so an empty section is not read as more than it is: the
importer looks at a behaviour's and a runnable's own content and one level inside the runnables,
the data type mapping references and the port API options — what it does not select *inside* an
event, an access or a mapping reference is still not reported. A runnable's description is carried
and a behaviour's own documentation is named (both below). A behaviour of a component SWCraft does
not import — a complex device driver, a service or a sensor-actuator component — is still reported
as one line for the whole component, and that line covers every description inside it.

**`swcraft import component` refuses more foreign files.** Every one of these lines stops a
component import, like every other skipped line of a component file: importing the component
without that content would lose it. A component file another tool wrote that carries any of it, and
that 0.13.0 imported silently, is now refused, the lines named in the message and nothing written.
A component file SWCraft wrote carries none of it and imports as before.

## Every component says whether its behaviour can be stopped and restarted

A component has a new field, `handle_termination_and_restart` — the AUTOSAR attribute of the same
name on a component's behaviour, which an RTE generator reads. AUTOSAR 4.2.2 and 4.3.0 require it on
every behaviour, so SWCraft now requires it on every component that is not external:

```yaml
name: BrakeController
handle_termination_and_restart: no_support   # or can_be_terminated, can_be_terminated_and_restarted
```

- **Required.** A component without the field is reported by `swcraft check-model` — so `swcraft
  validate` stops there — and refused, with nothing written, by `swcraft generate arxml` (at either
  ARXML version), by `--component` and `--all-components` (which lists it as failed and goes on)
  and by every change the assistant makes. The sentence names the component and the three values:
  *SWC 'ExampleSWC' sets no handle_termination_and_restart: every behaviour SWCraft writes carries
  HANDLE-TERMINATION-AND-RESTART, which AUTOSAR 4.2.2 and 4.3.0 require (multiplicity 1). Set it to
  no_support, can_be_terminated or can_be_terminated_and_restarted.* SWCraft never chooses the value
  for you. The licensed schemas declare the element optional, so a schema check alone would never
  have seen it missing.
- **Imported from every export.** `swcraft import model` and `swcraft import component` read the
  value from the source's `HANDLE-TERMINATION-AND-RESTART`, all three values; a value outside the
  three is a skipped line. A source whose behaviour states no
  value still imports — neither import refuses it, and neither import report names the components
  left without a value — and leaves the component without one, and then `swcraft check-model`
  reports it: choose the value and write it in.
- **Written as you set it.** The generated ARXML carries `HANDLE-TERMINATION-AND-RESTART` with the
  model's value on every component's behaviour.
