- **`no_support` is a declaration, and it is kept.** It is written to the file and to the ARXML
  like the other two values. What SWCraft does not do is write it for you.
- **A project imported before 0.14.0 has no value** and is refused until it is re-imported or the
  field is set by hand (*Upgrading a project*, below).
- **The assistant** is instructed to give a component it creates `no_support` unless you say
  otherwise, and to say which value it chose. Whether a model follows that instruction is not
  tested; a change that creates a component without the value is refused with the sentence above
  either way. A change it proposes for a project that still has components without the value is
  refused, naming all of them, until they have one.
- **`import component --update` keeps your value** when the file it reads carries no
  `HANDLE-TERMINATION-AND-RESTART` — which is true of every component file an earlier release wrote
  — and says so in one line of the report: *HANDLE-TERMINATION-AND-RESTART preserved from target
  (<value>): source element absent; absence does not request clearing this field.* A file that
  states a value replaces yours. A file cannot ask for the value to be cleared: edit the project for
  that.
- **Not on an external component.** An external component (`external: true`) has no behaviour in
  the generated ARXML, so a value there would be dropped: `swcraft check-model` reports it and
  `swcraft generate arxml` refuses it.

## A runnable may not take the name of an event its component generates

The generated ARXML names each event after what starts it — `TMT_{runnable}` for a timing event,
`IT_{runnable}` for the start-up event, `OIT_{port}_{operation}` for an operation event, numbered
where two would clash — unless the event states its own `name` (above). A runnable and those events
sit side by side in one behaviour, where AUTOSAR requires every name to be unique ignoring case. A
runnable called `TMT_Monitor` beside a timing event on runnable `Monitor` therefore produced an ARXML
file with one name twice, and nothing noticed.

Now `swcraft check-model` reports it — one finding per such runnable, naming the events it collides
with, compared ignoring case and against the names the ARXML really carries: a stated name as it is
written, a derived one numbered as it is written. `swcraft generate arxml` — the whole project,
`--component` and `--all-components` alike — and the assistant's edits refuse it with the same
sentence and nothing written; `swcraft import component` refuses a file whose component would produce
it — with `--update` also when the project's own operation events, kept because the file states
none, would. Rename the runnable, or state the event's `name`.

## One name per name space, ignoring case

AUTOSAR requires every name in the generated file to be unique, ignoring case, among the names that
share its *name space* — the nearest element above it that has a name of its own. The lists a file
groups names into (ports, runnables, events, members, connectors) are not name spaces: all the lists
of one element share one. SWCraft used to compare names exactly, list by list, and only a runnable
against its component's events ignoring case (above). Two ports `pOut` and `POUT`, or a composition
port and a member both called `Brake`, passed `swcraft check-model` and were written with one name
twice.

Now one check judges every name space of the generated file, by the names the file really carries —
a stated name as it is written, a derived one as SWCraft derives it:

- a component's ports, together with the name its behaviour is written with — its `behavior_name`,
  or `{component}_InternalBehavior` where it states none;
- a behaviour's runnables and events, the derived events by the numbered names the file really
  carries;
- a runnable's access points, across its three lists;
- an interface's data elements or operations, and an operation's arguments;
- a record's fields and an implementation record's elements;
- a composition's ports, members, delegations and the connectors drawn inside it, all in one;
- each package the file declares its elements in (below): the elements and the names SWCraft
  generates for them, and the names of its sub-packages.

It reports two things: names that differ **only in case**, and **one name in two lists** of one
element. `swcraft check-model` reports each group once, naming the name space and every name with
its list:

```text
SWC 'ExampleSWC' holds names equal ignoring case: 'POUT' (ports), 'pOut' (ports) -- AUTOSAR requires
a SHORT-NAME to be unique ignoring case within its name space ([constr_2508]); rename all but one.
```

A group that holds a generated event name adds *rename a port, an operation or a runnable, or state
an event's name*; one that holds a behaviour's generated name adds *rename the port, or state
behavior_name*; one in a package adds *set package on one of them to place it in a sub-package, or
rename it*. `swcraft generate arxml` — the whole project, `--component` and `--all-components` —
refuses the same groups with the same sentence and writes nothing; for a pair in one package it
refuses while it builds the document, naming the package, both spellings and the same rule, before
any connector it would otherwise report first. The assistant's edits are refused the same way, and
`swcraft import component` refuses a file whose component, interfaces or types would produce such a
group — with `--update`, also one that the project's own access lists or operation events, kept
because the file states none, would produce.

**What it does not judge**, so that a clean run is not read as more than it is: the same name twice
in **one** list is still the duplicate check that list always had (a duplicate port, runnable, data
element, member and the rest), and a runnable against an event is still the check above — each
reports as before; two events written with exactly one name are reported by the duplicate-event
check. Two elements of one kind with exactly the same name are the duplicate-name checks of their
folder, whatever the packages. An enumeration literal's label is not a name in this sense and is not
compared. Requirements, tasks, sequences and hardware are not written to the ARXML and are not
judged: two of their names that differ only in case matter only for the file names, as before.
`swcraft import model` still imports such a pair from an export that carries one, and `swcraft
check-model` then reports it; a name the import would state and that would make such a pair is not
stated (above). In the shipped example and the showcase there is none below
the package level.

## Two elements whose names differ only in case are written into two packages

AUTOSAR forbids two elements of one package whose names differ only in case: *"elements with
shortName "X" and "x" are considered the same and shall not exist in the same package"*. SWCraft
0.11.0 to 0.13.0 wrote every data type and mapping set into one `/DataTypes`, and an export may
keep an application type `Flag_T` and a base type `flag_t` in two packages of its own, so an
import could produce such pairs, all data types. Since this
release every layer of the data description has a package of its own — `/DataTypes/Application`,
`/DataTypes/Implementation`, `/DataTypes/Base`, `/DataTypes/Units`, `/DataTypes/CompuMethods`,
`/DataTypes/Constraints` and `/DataTypes/MappingSets` — so a pair from two layers no longer meets at
all. Every interface is still written into `/PortInterfaces` and every component and composition
into `/ComponentTypes`, and a pair inside one of those packages, or inside one layer's package, still
needs a place of its own.

**A new optional field, `package`, places an element in a sub-package** of the package it is written
in — `/DataTypes/Implementation/{package}/{name}`, `/PortInterfaces/{package}/{name}`,
`/ComponentTypes/{package}/{name}` and so on. Every element kind written into one of those packages
has it: a component, a composition, both interface kinds, every data type kind but the external one,
a mapping set, a unit, a computation method and a data constraint. The value is one name, never a
path, and it must be a legal AUTOSAR name; one that is not is reported by `swcraft check-model` and
refused by `swcraft generate arxml` and the assistant. The names SWCraft generates for an element go
with it — an enumeration's computation method, an application type's unit, conversion and range, a
value type's range, an interface's initial values, a component's implementation and behaviour.

```yaml
# model/data_types/base/flag_t~1.yaml
name: flag_t
kind: base_type
# … the type's other fields, unchanged
package: VendorTypes
```

- **An import records it in two cases.** `swcraft import model` and `swcraft import component` give
  `package` to one member of each pair whose two spellings the source keeps in two packages and that
  would otherwise share one package of the generated file. The member that stays where it is is the
  one already declared directly in that package — the layout SWCraft writes, so a file SWCraft
  generated imports back with its placement unchanged; when neither is, it is the one whose source
  path sorts first — on a first import of a foreign file that is the member with the plain file name,
  and the other, the one whose file carries the `~` suffix, is placed. The sub-package is named after
  the moving member's own source package, its last segment (`VendorTypes` for
  `/…/VendorTypes/flag_t`); when that name is taken it becomes `VendorTypes_2`, and when it is no
  legal AUTOSAR name, `CaseVariant`, with the report naming the segment it could not use. And both
  imports record the `package` of any element they find exactly one level below the package SWCraft
  writes its kind into — `/ComponentTypes/Body/Wiper`, say, records `package: Body` — which is where
  SWCraft's own file places an element with a `package`, twin or not.
- **The report says so** for the first case, in a block of its own above the skipped list — *Placed
  in a sub-package to keep a case-insensitive name unique* — one line per element, naming the
  element, its source path and where it is placed. Nothing is skipped for it, and no skipped count
  moves.
- **What moves in the ARXML is that element's path and every reference to it**, and nothing else. No
  name changes, no reference in the model changes, and no file is renamed.
  Importing a generated file into a fresh project records the same placement again, and one more
  round — generate, import, generate — gives the same model, element for element, and a
  byte-identical file. (The import of an export itself and the import of SWCraft's file are not the
  same model: they can differ, for example by the order of a component's ports in component files.)
- **You may set it yourself**, on any of those elements, in the file or through the assistant — it
  is how a pair you wrote yourself is repaired without renaming anything. Setting it moves that
  element's path in the generated ARXML, and nothing else, and both imports read it back from the
  generated file.
- **Two spellings in one source package** are the export's own defect, and there is no second package
  to tell them apart by: `swcraft import model` keeps the first by source path and lists the other
  under *Defects of the export*, citing `[constr_2508]`; `swcraft import component` refuses the file.
- **A name that differs only in case from one SWCraft generates** — a declared type
  `gear_t_compumethod` beside the `Gear_T_CompuMethod` an enumeration `Gear_T` generates, say — is now
  renamed by `swcraft import model`, and refused by `swcraft import component`, exactly as an equal
  one always was.
- **`swcraft import component`** keeps the sub-package a SWCraft-written component file places an
  element in; places an incoming type or interface that differs only in case from one the project
  already has, by its source package, and never moves the project's own; and refuses the file when
  that incoming element sits directly in the package SWCraft writes it into, naming the project's
  element you can place first. `--update` keeps the project component's `package`, and a shared type
  or interface that differs from the project's only in `package` is reused as it stands.
- **`swcraft generate arxml --all-components` exports both components of such a pair.** Two
  components whose names differ only in case, each in a package of its own, would have had one file
  name, `<name>.arxml`, which a filesystem that ignores case (macOS, Windows) holds as one file, so
  0.13.0 listed both as failed and wrote neither. Both are now written: the name that sorts first
  (capitals before small letters) keeps `<name>.arxml`, the other takes `<name>~1.arxml` — the
  suffix a model file takes for the same reason — and `export-summary.json` names each component's
  file. Only the file name carries the suffix; every name inside the file is the component's own. A
  component with no such twin keeps `<name>.arxml`.
- **`swcraft generate arxml --component` without `--output` names the file the same way.** Its
  default, `<dist_root>/components/<name>.arxml`, becomes `<name>~1.arxml` for the component that
  takes the suffix in `--all-components`, so exporting both members of a pair one by one leaves two
  files instead of one holding whichever was exported last, and a single export into the batch's
  directory rewrites that component's own file, never its twin's. The assistant's `export_component`
  tool and the VS Code *Export Component* command use the same default. A path you give with
  `--output` (or the tool's `output_path`) is used exactly as you give it.

**What this does not reach.** One level of sub-package only. The sub-package keeps the last segment of
the source package and nothing more of its path. An import reads a `package` back from the path's
shape alone, so a foreign export whose own package tree happens to be named like SWCraft's
(`/ComponentTypes/X/Y`) is read as SWCraft's layout too. A file an earlier release of SWCraft
generated declares its data types at `/DataTypes/{name}` or `/DataTypes/{package}/{name}`, which is
not this release's layout: it is imported like any foreign file, and a `package` it records is not
recovered, with no line saying so. Placement is recorded per import: a fresh `swcraft import model
--force` from a source that has since gained a twin can place the other member, which moves that
element's path; nothing else ever re-places a project. A 0.13.0 model of an enumeration, record,
array, component, composition, interface or mapping set that carried a stray `package:` key had it
ignored; from this release it is read, and places the element or is refused. `--all-components`
compares only the file names of one run: a file an earlier run left in the output directory is
replaced when a name of this run is the same ignoring case, is never removed, and on a filesystem that
ignores case keeps the spelling it had — so after `Foo` joins a project whose last run wrote
`foo.arxml`, `Foo`'s export is written into that file and `foo`'s into `foo~1.arxml`. Read the file
names from `export-summary.json`, never from the component names. The same holds for `--component`'s
default, which follows the model's names as they are when it runs: a twin added later moves the other
member's default to `<name>~1.arxml`, an earlier file is left where it is, and a path given with
`--output` is checked against nothing.

## Every named member can carry a description

A runnable, a data element, an operation, an argument, an enumeration literal, a record field and an
implementation record's element each gain an optional `description`, like the one every other element
already has. It is left out of the file while it is empty.

- **Imported.** Both imports carry the `DESC` of those seven, and of a composition member, a
  connector and a delegation, which had the field but whose `DESC` was never read: runnable descriptions and enumeration
  literal descriptions among them. Other runnable descriptions can belong to
  components SWCraft does not import (complex device drivers, services and a sensor-actuator
  component), each covered by that component's own skipped line; other literal descriptions can sit
  on the computation methods the import does not create — those it lists as a defect of the export
  and those that conflict — each a skipped line of its own. The text is read
  exactly as the export holds it, surrounding spaces included.
- **Written to ARXML.** Every description is written as the element's `DESC` — an enumeration
  literal's on its computation scale — exactly as the model holds it (*The generated file keeps
  every value the model holds*, above). A description you write in SWCraft therefore reaches the
  next tool through the whole-project file and through a component file alike.
- **Named where the model has no place for it.** An event's or an access point's `DESC`, and an
  array element's, are each one skipped line under *Not supported by SWCraft*. So is the `DESC` of a
  computation method, unit or data constraint the import reads into the type that names it rather
  than creating an element of it, when its text differs from the type's own description (which is
  carried); a unit, computation method or data constraint the import creates as an element carries
  its own description. When two declarations of one name are merged, a member's description the kept
  declaration does not carry is one line too, and so is one that differs from the kept one only in
  surrounding spaces.
- **`swcraft import component` refuses a foreign file carrying one of those skipped lines**, as it
  refuses every skipped line of a component file. A file SWCraft wrote carries no such `DESC`.
- **`--update` compares the component's own description, each port's and each runnable's.** A file
  whose part carries a different, non-empty description is a difference: `--update` takes the file's
  text, and without it the import stops on the conflict, naming the parts. A part whose description
  in the file is empty — every component file 0.13.0 or earlier wrote — keeps the project's text,
  and the report says so in one line per part: *DESC of runnable '…' preserved from target: source
  element carries none* (or *of component '…'*, *of port '…'*). An empty description in a file never
  clears yours.
- **A description of a shared type, interface, unit, computation method or data constraint the
  project already has is not taken**: the project's definition is kept as it stands. Each such text
  is one line under *Descriptions not taken from the file*, which reports and does not stop the
  import.

**What this does not reach.** A `DESC` is read as its first language block. A second language block,
inline markup inside it, or a language other than `FOR-ALL` on a text that is written back is named
in the report — under *Not supported by SWCraft*, and in `swcraft import component`'s *Not carried
from the file* — rather than carried. A `DESC` on an element the import
skips is covered by that element's own skipped line and not named again: the
texts of inter-runnable variables, per-instance parameters, parameter-interface parameters, mode
declarations, mode declaration groups and the skipped component types' own (complex device drivers,
services, a sensor-actuator component), for example. The
`DESC` of a computation method, unit or data constraint read into its type is not reported when it
equals the type's own description: it is the same text, and the type's copy is carried.

## A behaviour's and a runnable's own documentation is named

A behaviour's long name, category, introduction, annotations and description, and a runnable's long
name, category, introduction and annotations, are content SWCraft does not carry. Each one that holds
text is now one skipped line under *Not supported by SWCraft* — *LONG-NAME of a SWC-INTERNAL-BEHAVIOR
is documentation SWCraft does not carry -- not imported or preserved* — where it used to be dropped
without a word; one line per element, not per language block, and none for an empty one. A
behaviour's administrative data is handled as before. Every such line stops `swcraft import
component`, so a foreign component file carrying one is refused.

The same documentation on any **other** element — its short name fragments, a long name (but a
composition's, which is its title), an introduction or annotations — and an element's `UUID` are now
named too, one line each under *Not supported by SWCraft*: *UUID not carried: SWCraft carries no UUID
of an element -- not imported or preserved*. So is a package's own content: its description, long
name, category, administrative data and the rest, beside the elements it holds. Those lines document
and do not stop `swcraft import component`, which prints them under *Not carried from the file* and
goes on.

## The import report says whose problem each skipped element is

The skipped-element list of `swcraft import model` was one flat list, most frequent first, and it
mixed three different things a reader could not tell apart. It is now three sections, each printed
only when it counts something, in this order:

1. **Defects of the export** — the file breaks a rule of the AUTOSAR standard, and the line cites
   the rule. The fix belongs to whoever made the file.
2. **Not supported by SWCraft** — SWCraft's own gaps, or SWCraft's own stricter rules. The fix is
   SWCraft's.
3. **Outside the file** — the file references content it does not declare. The fix is to bring the
   file that declares it; until then the external elements stand in for it.

With that, `swcraft import model --dry-run` is a check of a tool export that writes nothing and says
of each line who has to act on it. The summary line carries the three counts, all of them printed,
and `--verbose` still lists every element under its line:

```text
SKIPPED 5 elements (export defects 3, not supported by SWCraft 1, outside the file 1)
...
Skipped elements, one line per reason (--verbose lists each element):
Defects of the export (3; the file breaks a rule of the standard, cited):
  - 2 × ASSEMBLY-SW-CONNECTOR (R4.2.2 [TPS_GST_00162]): requester end: unresolved reference ...
  - 1 × DELEGATION-SW-CONNECTOR (R4.2.2 [constr_1086]): duplicate delegation link ...
Not supported by SWCraft (1):
  - 1 × ADMIN-DATA: ADMIN-DATA/SDG vendor metadata on ...
Outside the file (1; the file references content it does not declare):
  - 1 × SYNCHRONOUS-SERVER-CALL-POINT: ...
```

An import that skipped nothing still prints `SKIPPED 0 elements` and no list.

**A line is a defect of the export only when the standard is cited for it**, and every citation was
read in the text of both releases. Each is a rule of the standard but one: a symbol that is not a C
identifier cites the table that defines the type a symbol has, `[GST primitive CIdentifier]` — the
pattern is that type's definition, both AUTOSAR schemas enforce it, and no rule of either release
restates it. The citations are:

| Citation | What the file does |
|---|---|
| `[TPS_GST_00162]` | a connector's end names a port that is not a port of the component the end goes through |
| `[constr_2530]` | a connector's end goes through a component that is not a member of the composition, or an access names a port of another component |
| `[constr_1086]` | two connectors, or two delegations, connect the same pair of ports |
| `[constr_1032]` | a delegation connects a provide port with a require port |
| `[constr_1088]` | a delegation's outer port belongs to another composition |
| `[TPS_SWCT_01113]` | an assembly connects two ports of one direction, whatever their interfaces |
| `[constr_1036]` | an assembly connects two ports of the same direction, one of a sender-receiver and one of a client-server interface |
| `[constr_2508]` | two elements of one parent share a name, or one path is declared twice in the file |
| `[constr_1221]` | a data element's initial value under an application primitive type is not an application value — an enumeration's value given as a number, say — or an enumeration's value matches none of its literals |
| `[constr_1385]` | a data element's initial value under an implementation type is given as an application value |
| `[constr_1225]` | a data element's initial value under an implementation type that references a table is not a text value naming one of its entries |
| `[constr_1284]` | a text value is given under a type that references no table |
| `[TPS_GST_00020]` | a data prototype, a record field or an array element is typed by a base type, or a record field or an array element by an implementation type |
| `[TPS_GST_00057]` | an element has a missing or blank short name |
| `[constr_1017]` | a queued data element states a calibration access other than not accessible |
| `[TPS_SWCT_01219]` | a component's require port defines no queued receiver com-spec for a queued data element of its interface |
| `[constr_1174]` | a composition owns a port typed by a service interface |
| `[constr_1277]` | a runnable reads a queued data element by value |
| `[constr_2025]` | two runnables of one component state the same symbol |
| `[GST primitive CIdentifier]` | a runnable's symbol is not a C identifier |
| `[constr_1375]` | a scale of a `LINEAR` computation method states a label |

**The citation names the release the file declares**, read from its schema location:
`(R4.2.2 [constr_1086])` for an AUTOSAR 4.2.2 export, `(R4.3.0 [constr_1086])` for a 4.3.0 one —
every rule above has the same id and the same text in both, with two qualifications: `[constr_1284]`
names two more table categories in 4.2.2 than in 4.3.0 and is cited only where both releases forbid
the text value, and `[constr_1375]` names its table by each release's own number. A file that
declares any other schema, or none, is judged against 4.3.0, the later of the two releases SWCraft
writes, and the section's heading says so and names what the file declared: `…; cited from R4.3.0 —
the file declares AUTOSAR_00051.xsd):` or `…; cited from R4.3.0 — the file declares no schema):`.
SWCraft does not claim to know a later release's ids. The line for two runnables of one symbol also
names, as support and with no release, the RTE specification's `[SWS_Rte_03527]`, which was read in
its R22-11 text only.

**The count line for connectors reaching an external component** cites the same way — the file's own
release and `[TPS_GST_00162]`, the rule that a connector's end is the path from the component to its
port — and points at the section that lists them. The skip reason itself carries no citation, so each
one is printed once.

**A file that carries variation points** is judged per file for a repeated name: its alternatives
may legitimately share one, and SWCraft binds no variant, so every repeated name of such a file is in
section 2 with a sentence saying why, a genuine duplicate included.

**A line skipped only because an earlier element was skipped** — an access behind a skipped port, a
connector behind a skipped component — lands in the section of the element that caused it, and its
reason names that element. Such a line in section 1 therefore cites the rule its cause breaks, not
one it breaks itself.

The defects of the export it sorts include connector ends on an external component naming a port of another
path (`[TPS_GST_00162]`), initial values of an enumeration given as a number (`[constr_1221]`),
connections repeated between one pair of ports (`[constr_1086]`), ends through a component that is
not a member (`[constr_2530]`), accesses declared twice (`[constr_2508]`), assemblies of two
ports of one direction (`[TPS_SWCT_01113]`), delegations between a provide and a require port
(`[constr_1032]`) and labels on scales of `LINEAR` computation methods (`[constr_1375]`). These
totals are not comparable with an earlier import's: during this release lines arrived (the behaviour
content above, the initial values) and many more went (every element SWCraft now carries — the names
it used to derive, the units, computation methods and data constraints, the members an external
interface lists); *If you import exports*, below, lists them.

**Some lines look like defects of the export and stay in section 2**, because the standard allows
them. Such a line is:

- a port with no interface reference (with delegations behind them): the
  standardized schema does not enforce the reference, so that a file may carry partial information,
  and SWCraft cannot import a port without an interface.

**What this does not reach.** The sorting was checked against real tool exports the maintainer holds privately; a reason they did not produce is sorted by
the same rules without a measured case. A line missing from section 1 is not a statement that the export is correct there —
the port above is the known case, and what SWCraft does not read (basic software configuration,
modes, calibration) is not looked at at all. Only the skipped list is sorted: the blocks above it
keep their own headings. And an assembly of a sender-receiver and a client-server port whose
directions do pair up is not skipped, so it is not in the list: it is imported, and
`swcraft check-model` reports it.

**Three rules of the table name something that is imported, not skipped**: `[TPS_SWCT_01219]`,
`[constr_1174]` and `[constr_1277]`. Each element of such a file is valid on its own, so the import
carries it exactly as the file states it, and the model it writes is one `swcraft check-model` and
`swcraft generate arxml` refuse. The line says so and names the check: a queued data element received
through a port that states no queue length for it, a composition's port typed by a service
interface, and a queued data element read by value. A queued receiver com-spec that is present and
states no queue length is the same line in section 2: the com-spec is defined, so no quoted rule is
broken, and SWCraft does not pick a queue length for you.
Because these lines count among the skipped elements, a script that reads `SKIPPED` as *left out*
should match on the line's text instead.

**Nothing about the exit code or what is written changes.** `--dry-run` writes nothing, and an
import that succeeds exits 0 however many defects of the export it names.

**`swcraft import component`** groups the lines of its refusal message the same way — each non-empty
section's heading, then its lines — and a defect's line carries its citation after the element's
path. Which files it refuses does not change; the report's own list of skipped out-of-scope elements
is unchanged.

## Every model file is read once, by libyaml

Every YAML file SWCraft reads — each element of the model, `swcraft.yaml`, a scenario file — is now
read by libyaml, the C parser PyYAML ships with, and each command reads each file once, where it used
to parse the same file again for every check that needed it. A command answers in a fraction of the
time; what it answers is the same.

**Checked** against real tool exports the maintainer holds privately, on macOS with CPython 3.11,
before and after this change (both inside this release's development; 0.13.0 itself was not
measured): `swcraft check-model`, `swcraft validate`, `swcraft generate arxml` and a run of requests
to the assistant's server answer in a fraction of the time they took, and
one `check-model` parses each file once instead of many times.

The parse count after the change is the number of distinct files — every model file and the
manifest, once each. The price is memory: a `check-model` on a large project peaks somewhat
higher, and the assistant's server about as much, for the parsed files it now keeps for the
command.

**libyaml follows the YAML specification where PyYAML's own Python parser did not**, so a few
hand-written shapes read differently. SWCraft's writers produce none of them, so a file SWCraft wrote
is not affected.

- **Now read**, where 0.13.0 refused the file: a tab used as separation (`a:`, a tab and `1` on one line, a trailing tab), a
  block-scalar header followed directly by `#`, and a `?` inside a plain scalar in flow context.
  `swcraft init --name` accepts a name with a tab inside it.
- **Now read to another value**: a lone `!` tag (`a: !`) reads as an empty string, where it read as
  nothing; and a byte order mark at the start of a line before a document's first node is dropped as
  the byte order mark it is, where it was read into the first key.
- **Now refused**, where 0.13.0 read the file. Two follow the specification: an escaped surrogate in
  a double-quoted string (`"\uD800"`, `"\uD83D\uDE00"`), and a byte order mark inside a document.
  Four are libyaml's own and depart from it: a tab after the indentation on a block scalar's first
  lines (`description: |` followed by a line `  \tcode`), a value left out directly before a flow
  indicator (`{a:}`, `[a:, b]`), an explicit `?` pair in flow with both sides empty (`[? ]`), and a
  reserved directive such as `%FOO bar`. Such a file fails `swcraft check-model` and
  `swcraft validate` with libyaml's message, naming the file, and the assistant's server answers
  that the element cannot be read, naming it, never the parser's text. Put spaces where the tab is,
  write an explicit `null` or a space after the colon, or delete the directive.
- **A file nested deeper than 1 000 collections is refused** with a YAML error naming the bound,
  before it is parsed: libyaml parses in C, and a deep enough document — about 47 600 levels on
  macOS — crashed the process. A document within the bound that is still too deep for a read to
  return — about 490 levels, where 0.13.0 stopped with *maximum recursion depth exceeded* — is
  refused the same way, naming its depth. 0.13.0 read at most about 494 levels, so neither refuses a
  file it read.
- **A refused file's message is libyaml's.** For a file both parsers refuse, the error's parser line
  is libyaml's text — `did not find expected node content` where 0.13.0 said `expected the node
  content, but found '<stream end>'` with a snippet. The exit code and what is written are unchanged.

A lone surrogate in a model value — which only a script using SWCraft's Python API can produce, since
the assistant's server refuses one in the request — is refused when the change is checked, with the
same answer the server gives for a model file that does not parse.

**libyaml is required.** It is part of the PyYAML package the workstation archive installs
(PyYAML 6.0.3 with libyaml 0.2.5). A Python environment whose PyYAML was built without it is refused
when SWCraft starts, with an error naming libyaml; SWCraft never falls back to the slower parser.

**What this does not reach:** the crash depth on Windows, whose stack is smaller, was not measured;
the figures above are one macOS host's. A file over the parse cache's size limit is read without being
kept, and a nesting the bound admits can still be too deep for a script of your own that walks the
returned value.

SWCraft's own test gate became faster with it: on the Linux runner the fast suite went from 1 717 to
1 065 seconds and the slow suite from 1 347 to 666; on the Windows runner from 2 699 to 2 343 and from
1 566 to 795. The packaging stage, which builds wheels rather than models, did not move.

## The archive

The workstation archive carries the same runtime payloads as 0.13.0, re-checked against the
publishers' own digests for this release and unmoved: Node.js 22.23.2, CPython 3.11.16 (the
python-build-standalone build of 2026-09-01), `elkjs` 0.12.0 inside the `swcraft-tools` package, and
the two extensions of the pack, Red Hat YAML 1.24.0 and Red Hat XML 0.29.3. The archive's PyYAML,
6.0.3, carries libyaml 0.2.5, which this release requires (*Every model file is read once, by
libyaml*, above). The macOS archive built for this release measures **143 214 867 bytes**, against
0.13.0's 142 459 026; the difference is the product's own wheels and the guide, which gained a page
and this note. The Linux and Windows archives are built on their own hosts and are measured by the
release build, not here.

## Smaller things

- **The guide has a new page, *The big picture***, between *Start here* and *Getting started*: where
  SWCraft stands in an AUTOSAR project (the VFB and the RTE), how the fifteen layers hold together as
  one model, what a model needs to build and what is a choice — the two views of a data type among
  them — and the three ways in (from nothing, from an export, with an assistant) and the one loop
  once you are in.
- **The writer's refusal of a repeated data type name names the name's layer**:
  *Duplicate data type names: 'uint8' (base_types)*, where it named the `data_types/` directory.
- **A number with a space between its sign and its digits** — `- 8` — is read as −8 in a field whose
  value is a formula (a limit, a coefficient, a value specification's value), since the standard's
  formula language allows the space there; a space inside the digits is still no number, and a field
  whose value is a plain number is unchanged.
- **Two declarations of one implementation value type whose bounds differ are a conflict.** Where an
  export declares one value type twice, the two are merged only when their ranges agree as well;
  otherwise both are listed under *Conflicting declarations*, as any other difference makes them.
- **Two declarations of one component whose client com-specs differ only in the operation they name
  are a conflict.** They used to be merged into one with no line; now both are listed under
  *Conflicting declarations*, as a server com-spec's operation already made them.
- **The *Merged declarations* block names more of what it drops**: a later composition's long name the
  kept title does not carry (*title not carried, from …*), and a description that differs from the
  kept one only in surrounding spaces or line breaks.
- **A queued receiver com-spec on a composition's require port** is one line for the whole com-spec —
  SWCraft writes none there — where it used to be a line about its queue length.
- **The assistant's runtime package no longer declares PyYAML.** `swcraft-agent` reads its scenario
  file through SWCraft's own reader and imports the YAML library nowhere, so its runtime dependency
  on it went; the workstation archive installs PyYAML for the other two packages as before.
- **A script that reads the model through the Python API** reads the data types from their layers:
  the snapshot no longer has one `data_types` collection, and carries the application,
  implementation and base types, the mapping sets and the three element layers each under its own
  layer's name.
- **Two fixes in how an import reads com-specs, older than this release.** A server com-spec on a composition's port whose queue length is not 1 used to be written
  as 1 with no line; it is a report line now, on a port of a declared interface as on one of an
  external interface. And a client com-spec on a port of a declared interface that names no
  operation of its interface, or a second one for the same operation, used to be dropped with no
  line; it is a report line now.

## What this release was measured against

Real tool exports the maintainer holds privately, on macOS: imported, reported, checked, generated and validated against the licensed
AUTOSAR schemas at 4.2.2 and at 4.3.0. Each generated file was compared with the export it came
from, element by element: every difference had to be either named in the import report or one of a fixed,
reviewed list of differences that mean the same thing, that the report names, or that SWCraft adds
on purpose. No export was imported on Windows.

The whole gate also runs on the two self-hosted runners, Linux and Windows.
macOS is this note's own host; Windows was measured only on its runner.

## The model's contract is `8.0.0`

`contractVersion` moves from `7.4.0` to `8.0.0`, seven minors with a wording patch between the first
two, then a major. The minors are listed as they arrived; the major at the end renames and removes
identifiers, which is why a project's own tooling that names one has to follow it.

`7.5.0` is the first minor: eighteen identifiers are added and none
is removed or renamed. The two kinds `external_interface` and `external_type` arrive with five fields
each (`name`, `kind`, `external_ref`, `external_dest` and an optional `description`), and six
checks with them — the two that report a malformed external element, the one that reports an initial
value on an external type, the one that reports an external component whose `external_ref` starts
with `/DataTypes`, `/PortInterfaces` or `/ComponentTypes`, and the two that refuse a blank name or
one carrying a path separator, which every element kind has. Twelve existing checks now admit, name or read an external element,
eleven of them with a reworded description; each still reports exactly what it reported on a model
that holds none. The
reference pages of this guide list all of them.

`7.5.1` changes wording only: the description of an enumeration now says its type is written with
the category `VALUE` and its computation method with `TEXTTABLE`, which is what the generated ARXML
now carries. No field, check or name moves.

`7.6.0` is the second minor: one field is added and none is removed or renamed. A port of an
external component may now be declared with its name and direction alone, so a port's `interface`
becomes optional, and the new optional `observed_interface` records the interface the port's
neighbour is typed by — an observation that no check reads. The check that reports what an
external component may not declare now allows such a port and still reports one that carries an
`interface` or `measures`. On any other component a port without an `interface` is now read and
reported by `swcraft check-model`, where 0.13.0 refused to read the project at all.

`7.7.0` is the third minor: twelve identifiers are added and none is removed or renamed. A runnable's
`events` gain a third kind, `operation`, which names one of the component's own `provide` ports and
an operation of its client-server interface: a client's call of that operation starts the runnable.
A runnable also gains `concurrent`, whether it may be started again while it is still running, left
out of the file while it is `false`. Seven checks arrive with them: one refuses a blank port or
operation name when the file is read, and six are reported by `swcraft check-model`. The reference
pages of this guide list all of them.

`7.8.0` is the fourth minor: forty identifiers are added and none is removed or renamed. Three data
type kinds arrive for the implementation side of a type: `implementation_record` (a structure, whose
`elements` each carry a `name` and a `type`), `implementation_array` (an array of a fixed `length`,
with its `element_type` and its `element_name`) and `pointer` (a `target`). A reference type may now
rest on any of them, and a mapping set may pair a record with an implementation record and an array
with an implementation array; records and arrays still need no map. Twenty checks arrive with them:
ten refuse a blank name, type or target, an empty `elements` list or a `length` below one when the
file is read, and ten are reported by `swcraft check-model`. The reference pages of this guide list
all of them.

`7.9.0` is the fifth minor: one field and one check are added and none is removed or renamed. A component gains
`handle_termination_and_restart` — whether its behaviour may be stopped, or stopped and restarted:
`no_support`, `can_be_terminated` or `can_be_terminated_and_restarted`, with no default: a written
`no_support` is a declaration, kept and written, and `7.10.0` makes the value required on every
component that is not external. An external component may not declare it, which the check that
reports what an external component may not declare now says. The check is the one that reports a
runnable named like an event its component generates, described above.

`7.10.0` is the sixth minor: twenty-two fields and two checks are added and none is removed or
renamed. A runnable, a data element, an operation, an argument, an enumeration literal, a record field
and an implementation record's element each gain an optional `description`, free text carried in the
model, exactly like the `description` every other element already has, and written to the generated
ARXML as the element's description since `7.11.0`, below; it is left out of the file while it is empty. Fifteen element kinds gain the optional `package` — a
component, a composition, both interface kinds, the ten data type kinds that are not external and the
mapping set. The check that reports a name that is not a legal AUTOSAR name now reads `package` too,
so a value such as `Platform Types` is reported like any other illegal name. The two checks are the
one name space rule and the required termination handling, both described above. One description is
reworded: `handle_termination_and_restart` now says that the value is required on every component
that is not external, and what happens when it is missing.

`7.11.0` is the seventh minor: thirty-six identifiers are added and none is removed or renamed. Both
interface kinds gain `is_service`, whether the interface is a service interface, left out of the file
while it is `false`. A data element gains `sw_impl_policy` (`standard` or `queued`) and
`sw_calibration_access` (`not_accessible`, `read_only` or `read_write`), both absent unless stated. A
port gains `com_specs`, one entry per data element of its interface recording the communication
attributes that differ from the defaults — `enable_update`, `alive_timeout`, `handle_never_received`,
`handle_timeout_type`, `handle_out_of_range`, `uses_end_to_end_protection`, for a queued element
`queue_length`, and the port's own initial value, `init` — and a timing event gains `disabled_modes`,
the modes it does not start its runnable in, each a port and the two ARXML paths of the mode. A
runnable gains `symbol`, the C name of its entry point. Both lists are left out of the file while they
are empty, and the two single values while they are unset, so every file written before them reads
and writes back unchanged. Five checks arrive with them,
each refusing a value when the file is read: a data element listed twice in one port's `com_specs`, a
negative `alive_timeout`, a `queue_length` below one, a disabled mode's path that is not an absolute
path of AUTOSAR names, and a `queued` data element with a `read_only` or `read_write` calibration
access. Ten more checks arrive, reported by `swcraft check-model`: a `com_specs` entry naming no
data element of its port's interface, or stating an attribute its port's direction or the element's
queuing has no place for; a queued data element received through a port that gives it no
`queue_length`, or read `by: value`; a disabled mode whose port is not a require port on an external
mode-switch interface; a composition port typed by an interface with `is_service: true`; an
application type with a `conversion` and no `unit`; a text XML cannot carry, described under
*Upgrading a project*; a `symbol` that is not a C identifier; and two runnables of one component
written with one symbol. Two connected or delegated ports are now also
incompatible when their interfaces differ in `is_service`, or when a data element is queued on one
side only. Twelve existing checks read more than they did: the check for a number that is not
finite reads `alive_timeout`, the check that reports what an external component may not declare reads
`com_specs`, the check that reports a declared type named like a generated `_Range` now also
reserves `{name}_Range` beside a value type that declares `value_min` or `value_max`, and the eight
checks of an initial value, with the one that reports a com-spec attribute a port has no place for,
now also judge a port's own `init`. Fifty
descriptions are reworded: every `description` of a kind that is written to ARXML now says it is
written as the element's `DESC` (an enumeration literal's on its computation scale), and the two
external kinds' that an external element writes nothing; a composition's `title` says that a title
other than the name is written as the long name; the fifteen `package` fields say that both imports
record the value for an element found in SWCraft's own package layout; a value type's says that its
declared bounds are written as a data constraint, and its `unit`'s why the unit alone is not written;
a timing event's now names its disabled modes; and an application type's `unit` and `conversion` say
that a conversion needs a unit. Twelve more texts are reworded with the port's `init` and the
runnable's `symbol`: the descriptions of a runnable, of a `com_specs` entry and of a data element's
`init`, and the summaries of the nine checks named above as now judging a port's own `init`. An
assistant that addresses a timing event by its `type` and `period` still reaches the same event: a
field at its default is not part of an event's identity.

**A limit is held exactly.** A value type's `value_min` and `value_max`, an application type's
`range` and a `conversion`'s `factor` and `offset` are still numbers, and an integer among them is
now kept as the integer it is, at any width: `value_max: 18446744073709551615`, the largest value
of a 64-bit unsigned type, is read, compared and written to ARXML with exactly those digits, where
0.13.0 held it as the floating-point number `18446744073709552000`. An initial value is compared against such a limit
exactly, so one past the limit is reported. The same holds on import: a limit of an export is
either carried exactly or not carried and named in the report — a limit written with more digits
than a floating-point number holds, such as `16777217.000000001`, is listed as *no model value
holds exactly* instead of being rounded, and a conversion with such a coefficient is imported
without the conversion. Two declarations of one type whose limits differ are a conflict however
small the difference. `swcraft query --where` and the assistant's edits compare such integers
exactly too: two limits one apart above 2^53 are two numbers, so `--where value_max=…` selects the
one you wrote, and an edit that changes only such a limit is reported and written. What this does
not reach: a limit written in a model file with a fraction or an exponent is a floating-point
number, as YAML reads it.

**An imported initial value is held exactly, or not imported.** An initial value written as an
integer is that integer at any width. One written with a fraction or an exponent is imported only
when a floating-point number holds it exactly; otherwise — `16777217.000000001`, or `1e-400`, which
is too small for a floating-point number and would become zero — the data element is imported
without its initial value and the import report names the value under *not supported*, where 0.13.0
imported the nearest floating-point number and said nothing. A project whose export states such a
value sees one more report line and one initial value fewer; set the value you intend in the model
file. A record or an array with one such member is not imported as a whole, like any other member
the import cannot read.

**An application type's `unit` is written and read exactly as the file holds it**, surrounding
spaces included, where 0.13.0 removed them on the way out and on the way in. A `unit` of spaces
alone is still no unit. An export that writes a unit's display name on a line of its own is
therefore imported with that line break; 0.13.0 removed it.

**A base type's `encoding` is read exactly as the export wrote it**, as it has always been written
exactly as the file holds it; 0.13.0 removed surrounding spaces and line breaks on the way in, so a
project holding `"  IEEE754  "` could not import its own component export. An `encoding` of spaces
alone is still no encoding. Only one comparison ignores that whitespace: where an export declares
one base type twice and the two differ in nothing else, they are still imported as one, the first
declaration's spelling is kept, and the import report now names the other spelling under the merged
declaration. An export that writes the encoding on a line of its own is therefore imported with that
line break; 0.13.0 removed it.

**A base type's `native_declaration` follows the same rule where one export declares the type
twice.** It was already read and written exactly. Two declarations whose native declarations differ
only in surrounding spaces or line breaks are still imported as one with the first declaration's
spelling, and the import report now names the other spelling under the merged declaration —
*native declaration spelling not carried, from …* — where 0.13.0 dropped it without a line.

**A conversion's scale limits are carried.** A `LINEAR` scale's `LOWER-LIMIT` and `UPPER-LIMIT` are
imported into the conversion's `limits` and written back as stated, rather than proved equal to the
type's physical bound and dropped (*A conversion states the stored values it applies to*, above).

`8.0.0` is the major. Against `7.11.0`, **139 identifiers are removed and 234 added**; the contract
now declares fifteen layers, fifty-eight element kinds, 295 fields and 272 checks. It was built in five
steps that all went into this one version, because none of them was ever released on its own:

- **The data types split into layers.** `layer:data_types` is now `layer:implementation_types`, and
  `layer:application_types` and `layer:base_types` are new; `layer:mapping_sets` moved under
  `data_types/`. Every identifier of a data type kind, its fields and its checks moved with the
  layer its kind moved to — `data_types.enum…` became `application_types.enum…`,
  `data_types.base_type…` became `base_types.base_type…`, `data_types.value_type…` became
  `implementation_types.value_type…`, and so on: 128 identifiers re-keyed in all. A data element's
  and an argument's `type` became `implementation_type`, beside the new `application_type`, with a
  check that exactly one of the two is stated and checks that refuse a blank one. Eleven checks are
  retired, each unreachable after the split (named in *The data types live in seven directories of
  their own*). The contract also records the two directories it retired, `data_types` and
  `mapping_sets`, which is what lets every read refuse a model still laid out in them.
- **The units, computation methods and data constraints arrived**: sixty-seven identifiers added,
  none removed — three layers, five kinds, thirty-one fields and twenty-eight checks. An
  enumeration's `literals` is no longer required, since it may name a table instead. Seven existing
  checks read the new elements as well.
- **An initial value follows its type's form.** No identifier is added or removed; the nine checks
  of an initial value now judge a value under a type that names a table as an entry's name, and three
  texts are reworded (see *An initial value is written in the form its type asks for*).
- **Names a model states, and the members an external interface lists**: fourteen identifiers
  added, none removed — a component's `behavior_name`, a `name` on each of the three kinds of event
  and on a read, a write and a call, an external interface's `operations` and `data_elements`, and
  five checks (a member listed twice in either list, a member of the wrong kind, an event name used
  twice, and a com-spec attribute a port on an external interface stub has no place for). Twelve
  existing checks read the new fields as well, among them the one that reports what an external
  component may not declare, which now also reports a `behavior_name` on one.
- **A conversion's scale limits**: sixteen identifiers added, none removed — four kinds (a `linear`'s
  and an inline `conversion`'s `limits` and their bounds), ten fields and two checks, each refusing
  limits whose lower bound is above the upper one, or equal to it with an `open` side, when the file is
  read. Three existing checks read the new fields: the one for a number that is not finite, and the two
  that compare connected or delegated ports' interfaces, which now compare a conversion's limits too.

**What a project pays for the major**: its files, once — the move into the seven directories and the
`type:` key renamed, both under *Upgrading a project* — and any script or tool of its own that names
an identifier the major renamed or removed, such as `layer:data_types`, a `data_types.…` check or
`rule:mapping-set.data-type-name-collision`. The reference pages of this guide list every current
identifier.

## Upgrading a project

### The model format changed, and one step of this is for every project with a data type

**Every project that declares a data type or a mapping set moves its files** — the one change of
this release that stops a project without a word about its content. Every component must also say
whether its behaviour can be stopped and restarted. The other causes below are rarer, and each names
the element it is about.

1. **Move the data types into their layers.** `swcraft init` scaffolds the seven directories; in an
   existing project create them, then move each file of `model/data_types/` by its `kind`, and the
   mapping sets out of `model/mapping_sets/`:

   ```sh
   mkdir -p model/data_types/application model/data_types/implementation model/data_types/base \
            model/data_types/mapping_sets model/data_types/units model/data_types/compu_methods \
            model/data_types/constraints
   ```

   - `enum`, `record`, `array`, `application_type` → `data_types/application/`;
   - `value_type`, `reference_type`, `implementation_record`, `implementation_array`, `pointer`,
     `external_type` → `data_types/implementation/`;
   - `base_type` → `data_types/base/`;
   - every file of `model/mapping_sets/` → `data_types/mapping_sets/`.

   A file keeps its name and its content; a base type keeps `kind: base_type`.
2. **Say which side each data element and argument names.** In every interface, replace `type:` by
   `implementation_type:` where it names an implementation type and by `application_type:` where it
   names an application type — exactly one of the two. SWCraft does not guess: one name may now be
   declared in both layers.
3. **Run `swcraft check-model`.**
4. **Commit the move on its own.** A revision on the old layout is refused like the working tree, so
   `swcraft diff` across that commit has nothing to compare on the old side; a diff between two
   revisions after it works as before.

Nothing converts a project on the old layout. A model that still holds an element file directly in
`data_types/` or in a `mapping_sets/` at the model root is refused on every read — `swcraft
check-model`, `validate`, the generators, the read-only commands (which exit non-zero here, as for
any project they cannot read) and the assistant's server alike — with one sentence that names the
directories and never a file:

```text
The model keeps its elements in a retired layout: 3 element files in 'data_types', a directory
contract 8.0.0 retired; they belong in 'data_types/application', 'data_types/implementation' or
'data_types/base'. Move each file into the directory of its layer; nothing converts a model on the
old layout.
```

For a revision the sentence begins *The model keeps its elements in a retired layout in revision
'HEAD~1'*, naming the revision as you passed it. A retired directory that is empty, or holds only
subdirectories and files that are not `.yaml`, is not refused. A data element or an argument that
still says `type:` is refused naming the element and the two keys it may use instead.

**A project imported from an export** is upgraded by importing the export afresh, which writes the
new layout; edits made to the earlier import are not carried over, and the project's own files that
the import does not write move by the steps above. A fresh import gives each type the name it has in
the export — the `{name}_impl` names an earlier import invented are gone — and creates the units,
computation methods and data constraints the export shares.

**Going back** across this release means going back to the old model as well: the files in their old
directories and every `implementation_type:` back to `type:`, which committing the move on its own
makes one revert.

### What else can stop a project that checked clean

**Two types whose conversions differ only in their scale limits are no longer interface-compatible.**
A connector or a delegation between ports whose data elements are typed so is reported by `swcraft
check-model`. No project before this release states a limit, so none meets it until one is added.

**A component with no `handle_termination_and_restart`** is reported by `swcraft check-model` and
refused by `swcraft generate arxml`, by the component export and by every change the assistant
makes. Choose per component:

- `no_support` — the behaviour cannot be stopped or restarted;
- `can_be_terminated` — it can be stopped;
- `can_be_terminated_and_restarted` — it can be stopped and started again.

Write it into each component's file:

```yaml
handle_termination_and_restart: no_support
```

A project imported from an export that states the value everywhere gets it back by a fresh import. A
source that omits it still needs this edit. SWCraft never picks a value for you. Through the
assistant, one change that sets the field on every component named in the refusal is the repair —
**in a session whose approved scope covers all of them, or no scope at all**; a narrower scope is
refused until the files are edited. A draft the assistant's server makes from a component file that
states no value needs the same change added before it is submitted.

**Two names in one component, behaviour, runnable, interface, operation, record or composition that
are equal ignoring case — or the same name in two of its lists, such as a composition port and a
member** — are reported and refused; rename all but one. The shipped
example and the showcase have none.

**Two elements of one package whose names differ only in case** — two types of one layer, two
interfaces, or two components and compositions — are reported and refused unless one of them is
placed in a sub-package. Since each data type layer has a package of its own, an application type
`Flag_T` and a base type `flag_t` no longer share one. Where your project holds such a pair, add one line to the file of one member:

```yaml
package: VendorTypes
```

The name and every reference stay; only that element's path in the generated ARXML moves. A fresh
import records the placement itself.

**An application type with a `conversion` and neither `unit` nor `unit_ref`** is reported by
`swcraft check-model`: the conversion is written as a computation method that must name a unit, and
SWCraft does not pick one for you. Declare the type's unit beside its conversion:

```yaml
unit: km/h
conversion:
  factor: 0.1
```

The shipped example, the showcase and the project `swcraft init` scaffolds have none.

**A declared type named `{X}_Range` beside a value type `X` that states `value_min` or
`value_max`** is reported: SWCraft now writes a value type's bounds as a range named `{X}_Range` in
the same package, so the two names collide. Rename the declared type.

**A text holding a character XML cannot carry** — a NUL or another control character other than
tab, line feed and carriage return, which a YAML file can hold through a double-quoted escape such
as `"\x07"` — is now reported by `swcraft check-model` in any element's `description`, a
composition's `title`, a base type's `native_declaration` or `encoding`, an application type's
`unit`, a unit's `display_name` and a table entry's `description`. Such a model was never written:
`swcraft generate arxml` already refused it and wrote nothing, and now names the element in its
refusal. SWCraft writes a text exactly as you hold it and never removes a character for you, so
remove it from the file. The shipped example and the project `swcraft init` scaffolds have none.

**Two rarer causes.** A runnable whose name, ignoring case, is one its component's generated events
also take is reported and refused, as described above; rename the runnable or state the event's
name. And an external component (`external: true`) whose `external_ref` starts with `/DataTypes`,
`/PortInterfaces` or `/ComponentTypes` is now reported by `swcraft check-model` and refused by
`swcraft generate arxml`. Those are the packages the generated ARXML declares the project's own
elements in, so every use of that component was written as a reference to one of them; give it the
path of the component in the file that really declares it. One refusal also changes its name without
changing its verdict: a mapping set that pairs a record or an array with a value type or a reference
type was reported as *mapping-set.unknown-application* and is now reported as
*mapping-set.incompatible-composite-map* — still refused, under the check that now owns the pair.

**What the generated files look like afterwards.** Expect the first build after the upgrade to
differ throughout. Every data type, mapping set and generated form moves into its layer's package,
with every reference to it (a model with no data type is the exception); no port carries
`PORT-API-OPTIONS` any more; each component's behaviour carries the
`HANDLE-TERMINATION-AND-RESTART` you set; each enumeration's category line changes; and what the
sections above describe as newly written — descriptions, long names, exact timing, a value type's
bounds, the members' categories, a runnable's symbol, the values in their type's form — appears where
the model holds it. The content of every element is otherwise what 0.13.0 wrote, checked on every
committed project; that is evidence over those projects rather than a proof over every model. A
project that keeps its generated ARXML under version control should commit that first build on its
own.

### If you import exports

Re-import, and read the report: it is the import that changed most in this release. A script that
parses the report should match on the headings and the counts, never on whole lines.

1. **Re-import and read the report.** Where 0.13.0 listed a reference under *Unresolved references*
   because the export declares the target nowhere, 0.14.0 usually imports an external element
   instead, and the section shrinks by exactly those references. Expect `swcraft check-model` to
   report far fewer findings, and `swcraft generate arxml` to succeed where it refused.
2. **Expect the new layout and new files.** An import writes the data description into its seven
   directories under `data_types/` (*The data types live in seven directories of their own*, above), external types into
   `data_types/implementation/` and external interfaces into `interfaces/`, one file per external
   element, and ports that name them where 0.13.0 wrote a path. Units, computation methods and data
   constraints arrive as elements of their own, with an *IMPORTED* line each for their count.
3. **The external element blocks.** A script should know the headings *External interface stubs*,
   *External type stubs* and *DEST disagreements*, and the `STUBBED` summary count. `UNRESOLVED`
   counts fewer references. An external interface now lists the operations and data elements the
   export reaches through it, so an access, a call, an operation event and a com-spec through a
   listed member are imported, and their *Outside the file* lines are gone; what is still skipped
   through an external interface — a com-spec of a mode-switch interface, an initial value on such a
   port's com-spec — names its own reason. An initial value whose type reaches an external type
   through reference types is left out with a line of its own. An external interface that
   takes an `_ext` suffix is listed with the renames.
4. **A component that reaches an external element cannot be exported on its own.** If your build
   exports every component, expect those to be listed as failed.
5. **Expect external components to gain ports, and their connectors to come back.** The skip reason
   *"which declares no port"* is gone; what is still skipped for an external component names its
   own reason — most often *target port path is not owned by the context component's type*, a
   defect of the export. A script that counted the old reason should count the new blocks instead:
   *External component stub ports*, *Stub ports not imported*, *Stub ports with no observed
   interface* and the line counting the connectors skipped as a defect of the export.
6. **Two declarations of one composition that differ only in a connector end's kind of port** — the
   `DEST` the end names, or whether a delegation goes through a providing or a requiring port — are
   listed under *Conflicting declarations*, where they used to be merged into one.
7. **Expect server runnables to gain `operation` events and `concurrent: true`**, and the skipped
   list to lose the *OPERATION-INVOKED-EVENT* lines of every event it now imports — what is still
   skipped names its own reason. Two declarations of one component that differ only in an operation
   event's port or operation, or in a runnable's concurrency, are listed under *Conflicting
   declarations*, where they used to be merged into one — an absent concurrency and `false` are one
   value, as they are written. A concurrency value that is none of `true`, `false`, `1` and `0` is a
   skipped line naming it. The report has a new heading, *Server queue lengths not carried*.
8. **Expect implementation structures, arrays and pointers to arrive** in `data_types/implementation/`,
   the skipped list to lose its *unsupported category* lines for them, and mapping sets to gain the
   entries that pair records and arrays; records and interfaces that used to be skipped are imported.
   The report has a new heading, *Data type maps kept that SWCraft's composite check refuses*.
9. **Expect no `{name}_impl` renames.** An application type and an implementation type that share a
   name are both imported under that name, one in each layer, and the rename lines for them are gone. The collapse of a bare pair onto its implementation member stays, and is
   listed where it was. A merge or
   conflict line names its element by its layer — `application_types/…`, `implementation_types/…`,
   `base_types/…` — where it said `data_types/…`.
10. **Expect the lines about the data description to move.** Gone: a unit's, a computation method's
    and a data constraint's *SHORT-NAME … not carried: SWCraft names it itself*, *… shared by N data
    types not carried as one*, an implementation type's *COMPU-METHOD-REF … not carried* (one stays,
    under a new sentence, for a type naming a table that cannot be an enumeration), a data
    constraint's *CONSTR-LEVEL … not carried*, and most of *TEXTTABLE compu-method not used by any
    imported enum type*. Moved: a label on a `LINEAR` computation method's scale is a defect of the
    export citing `[constr_1375]`. A unit, a computation method or a data
    constraint declared twice under one name now takes the merged-or-conflicting verdict a type takes.
11. **Expect the initial-value lines to change.** An initial value the import does not carry is one
    line under *Defects of the export* (its form breaks the rule it cites) or *Not supported by
    SWCraft*; a port's own value not carried, a value whose unit is not its type's, and a value written
    in the numerical form because its type is the implementation twin it collapsed to each have a
    line of their own (*An initial value is written in the form its type asks for*, above). The two
    port-level lines of 0.13.0 that refused a port's own value, and the element's own value with it,
    are gone.
12. **Expect the generated-name lines to go.** *SHORT-NAME … not carried: SWCraft names it itself*
    for a behaviour, an event or an access point is gone wherever the import states the source's name;
    a name it cannot state keeps the line,
    which now says why. *SYMBOL differs from the runnable's SHORT-NAME* is gone: the symbol is
    carried. A port API option carrying content is one line per option,
    tagged `PORT-API-OPTION` and keyed at the option's port.
13. **Expect many skipped lines about a behaviour's content**, one per kind of content the importer
    does not read (*What an import cannot carry from a component's behaviour is named*, above), and
    every component to gain `handle_termination_and_restart` where the export states it; one without
    it is reported by `swcraft check-model` until you set it.
14. **Expect the skipped list's text to move — a breaking change for a script that parses it.** The
    `SKIPPED` line gains the three section counts in parentheses, the list gains the three section
    headings, a defect's line carries its citation between the tag and the colon, the count line for
    connectors reaching an external component cites the file's own release instead of
    `R22-11 [constr_2626]`, and the connector skip reason itself no longer carries that citation. A
    reason that named several possible causes is now one line per cause, each naming its own. Set beside an
    earlier import's total, the difference is the lines above and says nothing by itself.
15. **Expect descriptions, and the lines about them.** Runnables, data elements, operations,
    arguments, enumeration literals, record fields, implementation elements, composition members,
    connectors and delegations gain the `description` the export gives them. A script should know
    the lines that name a description the model cannot hold, and those that name a behaviour's or a
    runnable's own documentation.
16. **Expect `package: …` only where a placement is needed.** An element is placed in a sub-package
    when two names of one layer differ only in case, and listed in the block *Placed in a sub-package
    to keep a case-insensitive name unique*.
17. **An octal number is read as octal.** A number the export writes with a leading zero, such as
    `010`, is eight — the notation the standard defines for it — where 0.13.0 read ten. A binary initial
    value (`0b11`) is now read, where it was refused. A signed hexadecimal or binary number (`-0x10`) in a
    field whose value is a plain integer or number — an application value's number, a base type's size,
    a constraint's level, a queue length — is now refused, since the standard writes a negative number
    there only in decimal or float notation; it is still read in a formula field such as a limit or a
    numerical value. A signed zero (`-0`, `+0`) in an integer field — a base type's size, a
    constraint's level, a queue length — is now refused too, since the standard writes zero there
    unsigned; in an application value's number it is still zero. A base type's size and a queue
    length are positive integers, which the standard writes with no sign at all, so `+8` and `-8`
    there are now refused as well; a constraint's level still reads `+8` as eight. A number with a leading zero that is not octal (`08`, `010.5`), which 0.13.0 read
    as decimal, is no longer read and is skipped with a line; `-010` is −8 in a formula field and
    unreadable in a plain one, and `+0x10` is now read in a formula field. A number, a true/false
    value or a named value padded with whitespace other than spaces, tabs and line breaks (a no-break
    space) is no longer read either: a limit and its interval type, a conversion's coefficient, a
    constraint's level, a queue length, a com-spec's flag, a runnable's concurrency, a category, a byte
    order, an alignment, an implementation or calibration policy, a scale's label and the other named
    values get the line their field gives any value it cannot read, and two otherwise equal
    declarations that differ by such a space are no longer merged. Spaces, tabs and line breaks around
    the value are still read. An interface's service flag follows the same rule, and a flag that is
    no true/false value at all — `yes`, or `true` padded with a no-break space — is never read as
    false: the interface is skipped with a line saying the flag could not be read as a true/false
    value, and its data elements or operations, its ports and their connectors are skipped with it,
    each with its own line. That holds for every skipped interface, whatever the reason — a blank
    name, a name already taken, a member it cannot import, no member left: each of its data
    elements, operations and arguments now gets a line naming the interface's reason, where it was
    skipped without one.
    A time value — a timing event's period, a runnable's minimum start interval, a com-spec's alive
    timeout — is read as the standard's floating-point number and nothing wider: a spelling only
    Python reads (`1_000`, a full-width digit, `infinity`, the same padding) is no longer read, and
    an unreadable time value is never read as `0`: it is reported, not silent. A runnable whose
    minimum start interval cannot be read as a number is skipped with a line saying so, where 0.13.0
    wrote it with the interval `0`; a timing event whose period cannot be read is skipped with a line
    that now says the text could not be read as a number, not that the period is absent; and the alive
    timeout is listed as a value the model cannot hold, as it was.
    A conversion's denominator is read in the notation of its coefficients: `0x1` or `+ 1` is the
    denominator one and the conversion is imported, and a spelling outside it (`001.0`) is not one.
    A project whose export writes any of them will see those values change
    on re-import. An initial value re-spelled from octal or binary is listed with the hexadecimal
    ones, in the report's section now headed *Init values re-spelled from hexadecimal, octal or binary
    to decimal* — a script that matches the old heading must match the new one.
18. **Expect a `LINEAR` conversion's limits in the imported files.** A computation method or an inline
    conversion gains `limits` where the export states them, where 0.13.0
    dropped a limit it could prove equal to the type's bound; a limit
    infinite on its own side is a descriptive line. Two computation
    methods of one name are compared by their limits' values: `100`, `0x64` and `100.0`, or no
    interval type and `CLOSED`, are one limit. A limit SWCraft holds exactly in one spelling only —
    above 2^53, written once as an integer and once with `.0` — makes two declarations, of a
    computation method or of a data constraint.
19. **A port API option with both features off is a descriptive line**, where it had none.

### If you exchange component files

Every component file this release writes carries one more line of SWCraft's own metadata, the
statement that it carries operation events and concurrency, so a component file differs from
0.13.0's by that line even for a component without an operation event. SWCraft 0.13.0 does not
know the line and refuses the whole file, so a component file this release writes cannot be imported
by 0.13.0 or earlier, whatever the component declares: exchange files with a project on 0.13.0 by
exporting from that project. Keep the project's own operation events safe when you update from an
older file: `--update` from a file without the statement keeps them, as described above, and a file
that has the statement is the truth for them.

**A component file now carries what the model holds**, and `swcraft import component` compares it:
the component's, its ports' and its runnables' descriptions, its timing exactly, a value type's bounds,
